entries.title: Defense attorney wants 'Broadview 6' prosecutor on the stand in CBP sex assault case: 'She hasn’t testified'
entries.summary: <p>It’s been three months since<b> </b>revelations of prosecutorial misconduct<b> </b>in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >case of the “Broadview Six”</a><b> </b>rocked the Dirksen Federal Courthouse, and there’s still been no hearing over allegations<b> </b>that cast unusual doubt on the credibility of U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros’ office.</p><p>So in a sign of the defense bar’s pent-up frustration, an attorney for a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/24/luis-uribe-customs-cbp-broadview-six" target="_blank" >accused of sexual assault</a> insisted Wednesday that Assistant U.S. Attorney Sheri<b> </b>Mecklenburg should testify under oath — and so should anyone who worked in the grand jury room with the veteran prosecutor at the center of the "Broadview Six" scandal.</p><p>“We don’t even know the level of inappropriate statements that were made to this grand jury by [Mecklenburg],” defense attorney<b> </b>Michael<b> </b>Clancy<b> </b>told<b> </b>U.S. District Judge Jorge<b> </b>Alonso. “We have no idea. Because she hasn’t testified. It hasn’t been disclosed.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" >What to know about the ‘Broadview Six’ scandal rocking Chicago’s federal courthouse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The nearly hour-long argument by Clancy came ahead of a pretrial conference<b> </b>in the case of CBP Officer Luis<b> </b>Uribe, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >accused of sexually assaulting<b> </b>women</a><b> </b>in Chicago’s suburbs in 2022. Uribe was indicted<b> </b>in December by the same grand jury<b> </b>that indicted the “Broadview Six,” though Uribe’s case was not handled by Mecklenburg.</p><p>Still, Clancy said Mecklenburg’s misconduct<b>, </b>which occurred in October, tainted the grand jury to the point that Uribe’s indictment should be thrown out.<b> </b>Clancy<b> </b>compared the grand jury on Wednesday to a pot of water.</p><p>He explained that, “once you put in some bad meat, into that water … you can take [out] all of the spoiled stuff … you can take [out] all of [Mecklenburg’s] conversations … all of her antics.”</p><p>But, he said, “the water’s still bad.”</p><p>And crucially, there are still questions about Mecklenburg’s conduct.</p><p>Alonso agreed Wednesday to review grand jury minutes<b> </b>from the Uribe case, but he declined to rule on Clancy’s motion to dismiss the indictment. Still, the defense attorney’s impassioned argument is indicative of the legal community’s desire to get to the bottom of what happened with Mecklenburg.</p><p>Assistant U.S. Attorneys Richard<b> </b>Rothblatt<b> </b>and<b> </b>Jonathan<b> </b>Shih<b> </b>accused Clancy of gamesmanship by bringing up the issue on the eve of Uribe’s Sept. 8 trial. Shih also said there’s no legal authority for Clancy’s argument.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/24/luis-uribe-customs-cbp-broadview-six" >CBP agent says feds’ ‘Broadview Six’ misconduct tainted his sexual assault case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>“There’s no concrete evidence,” Shih said. “There’s no indication that there’s any wrongdoing in this particular case. And absent that, there’s no basis for dismissal.”</p><p>Mecklenburg has been accused of three types of misconduct before the grand jury that indicted the “Broadview Six,” a group of Operation Midway Blitz protesters. She allegedly spoke to grand jurors outside the grand jury room<b> </b>and excused panel members who didn’t agree with the feds’ case.</p><p>She’s also accused of “vouching,”<b> </b>a forbidden practice in which prosecutors put their personal credibility on the line to support criminal charges.</p><p>The revelations prompted Boutros to drop the charges against the "Broadview Six." Meanwhile, similar allegations against Mecklenburg have surfaced in other cases.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" >U.S. District Judge April Perry</a><b> </b>presides over the “Broadview Six” case. She’s yet to rule on a defense request for sanctions<b> </b>and the appointment of an independent special counsel who could investigate<b> </b>Boutros and others for criminal contempt.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" >‘Broadview 6' judge has to decide whether to hold prosecutors accountable after exposing misconduct</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Perry is unlikely to rule until September. That's partly because prosecutors<b> </b>asked for<b> </b>two<b> </b>extensions in the briefing schedule, and defense attorneys asked for one.</p><p>Meanwhile, U.S. District Judge Sharon Johnson Coleman<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/10/hearing-in-loretto-hospital-case-could-address-claims-of-prosecutors-misconduct-if-feds-dont-drop-it" target="_blank" >threatened<b> </b>in June</a> to hold the kind of hearing being sought by Clancy. She presides over a case tied to Loretto Hospital that was once handled by Mecklenburg. Boutros’ office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/11/broadview-six-grand-jury-misconduct-federal-prosecutors-drop-charges-loretto-hospital-covid-fraud" target="_blank" >avoided that hearing</a><b> </b>by permanently dropping charges<b> </b>against two defendants.</p><p>Clancy brought that up, too. He complained to Alonso that the feds “dismissed cases so that [Mecklenburg] didn’t hit the stand, and wouldn’t hit the stand, and Mr. Boutros wouldn’t have to hit the stand.</p><p>“And that’s just wrong,”<b> </b>he said.</p><p>Clancy said he never would have expected Mecklenburg to engage in such alleged misconduct. He called the Chicago U.S. attorney’s office “a proud office that I’ve respected for 27 years.”</p><p>But now there are questions, he said. And<b> </b>Mecklenburg “is not an island.”<b> </b>She worked in the grand jury room with colleagues, and Clancy questioned whether she’d ever vouched for other prosecutors in the office.</p><p>“She is not a sole practitioner,” Clancy said. “She is not someone who acts alone.”</p>

entries.title: Miguel Vargas' 'unbelievably stable' skill set is pacing the White Sox offense
entries.summary: <p>Colson Montgomery whacked 21 homers in 71 games last year, Munetaka Murakami arrived as a generational Japanese slugger. In the White Sox lineup’s three-headed hydra that’s likely to produce three separate 30-homer seasons, Miguel Vargas is the member that would have been hardest to explain back in March.</p><p>Yet on the strength of a dominant August and a 13-game on-base streak he extended in Wednesday's 10-4 victory over the Rangers, Vargas now leads the Sox with an .861 OPS, in decidedly non-fluky fashion.</p><p>"Miggy's always had this unbelievably stable offensive base,” said bench coach Walker McKinven. “He makes excellent swing decisions. He's an above-average contact guy and the damage was sporadic but you saw the high ends of that, and you saw real power in there. This year in just trying to diagnose it simply, he's moving the bat faster, he swings the bat harder and he's maintained swing decisions and his contact ability.”</p><p>Where lighttower power has been a strength of both Montgomery and Murakami for years now, Vargas is the purer story of what a revamped White Sox hitting department can accomplish now when paired with a hitter willing to remake his body and swing.</p><p>To McKinven’s point, the rates Vargas makes contact or chases pitches out of the zone are remarkably similar to when he hit a miserable .104/.217/.170 after being acquired at the trade deadline in 2024. But where he once provided doubles power at best, Vargas has made some of the biggest gains in bat speed across the league after two-straight offseasons dedicated to adding strength. Now he’s a hitter worth pitching around, who takes his walks when the opposition tries exactly that.</p><p>“You find these little pockets and stretches where maybe he's just not being attacked as much, and he's not giving in,” said manager Will Venable. “That's just where Vargy has really found his consistency this year. He's just throwing out the same approach, the same swing every single day."</p><p>With Vargas running an OPS over 1.000 for August while Montgomery and Murakami scuffle, his raw ingredients sound like the recipe for a slump-proof hitter. Since he leads the American League with 91 runs scored, he’s closer than most.</p><p>But after swatting a titanic All-Star Game home run that announced his breakout to the world, Vargas slumped through the first 20 games after the break (.188/.275/.363, 26.3% strikeout rate). Vargas elevates the ball relentlessly, which puts a lot of pitches over the fence, but the way his swing path can become long, loopy and prone to popups, reminds Sox hitting coaches of struggles that have befallen their other boppers.</p><p>It’s just as the Sox grind through a punishing August slate, the 26-year-old Vargas sounds more like a grizzled five-year veteran (which he quietly is) when talking about finding a fix.</p><p>“At this point of the year, you just kind of know what is going on and the way your body feels every day, and you try to adjust,” Vargas told the Sun-Times. “[Hitting coaches Derek] Shomon and Joel [McKeithan] are always trying to put me in a better spot. They have been really consistent with me this year, when we talk about positions with my hands and attacking the ball.”</p><p>In a past two years full of impressive adjustments, negotiating how his body feels might be Vargas’ greatest trick. He’s sat just two games all season and could blow past his career-high in games played (138) next week. For a young Sox team negotiating the dog days of August, Vargas has been once more, unbelievably stable.</p><p>“Last year, playing my my full season in the big leagues, that helped me [to see] how important is recovery, sleep,” Vargas said. “You want to put your body where it's 100%. At this point, it's not gonna be 100% every day. But I want to just feel the best I can, where I'm giving my body that shot to do the best I can every day.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Tristan Peters homers for fifth-consecutive game, matching White Sox franchise record
entries.summary: <p>White Sox All-Star outfielder Tristan Peters said a funny thing a few hours before hitting a home run for the fifth consecutive game Wednesday night, matching a franchise record.</p><p>“I'm staying on my backside a little more,” Peters said. “Staying back, just letting the ball travel a little longer, letting me recognize pitches better.”</p><p>Normally this is the talk of a hitter who is trying to spank singles to the opposite field, a la Tony Gwynn.</p><p>Instead, for the fifth time in as many nights, Peters whacked a pitch over the fence to the pull side, this time a hanging slider from Rangers reliever Robby Ahlstrom. The fifth-inning blast and the streak put Peters in rare air in terms of White Sox history, occupied only by the likes of Frank Thomas (twice), Paul Konerko, A.J. Pierzynski, Carlos Lee, Greg Luzinski, Ron Kittle and–earlier this year–Munetaka Murakami.</p><p>For a 26-year-old rookie acquired for cash after being designated for assignment by the Rays last December, Peters’ breakout 2026 season is defined by wild pivots. But his latest one might still be his greatest. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/21/white-sox-tristan-peters-second-half-slump-all-star-game-brenton-doyle-davis-martin-kyle-teel-will-venable-derek-shomon-mets-luis-robert-jr" target="_blank" ><u>After suffering through a 4-for-48 slump in July</u></a> that allowed speculation that there were some fluky elements to his first half, Peters’ prodigious slugging while he works to track breaking balls better and chase less, are representative of a hitter who is sacrificing nothing, and hitting everything.</p><p>"When you hear things like that with guys, for me it sounds like he just trusts where he's at,” said manager Will Venable. “He trusts his swing, he's letting the ball travel. He's not feeling like he needs to rush or cheat to things and kind of expedite the decision part of it. Because he just has a nice move that he has confidence in and he trusts his swing. That's the best spot to be in as a hitter.”</p><p>Rather than receding, Peters is having the best offensive month of his major league career right as the White Sox offense is enduring slumps from Murakami and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/25/white-sox-shortstop-colson-montgomery-offensive-struggles-jake-burger-will-venable-derek-shomon-jacob-degrom-all-star-home-runs" target="_blank" ><u>Colson Montgomery</u></a>. He entered Wednesday hitting .322/.420/.661 in August, before singling, doubling and homering, as the Sox broke open a big lead in the rubber match against a playoff hopeful Texas team that entered the night tied for first place in the American League West.</p><p>On top of hitting for the cycle on July 10th against the Athletics, Peters has now fallen a triple short of repeating the feat in each of the past two nights. The second home run of this streak was Sunday’s walk-off blast against the Mets; Peters’ third walk-off plate appearance of the season.</p><p>With Sean Burke exiting after three innings and a career-high eight walks Wednesday night, giving way to a bullpen exhausted by 16 games in 16 days, and the Cleveland Guardians bearing down on them with a seven-game winning streak, this surprising young Sox team is being tested as much as ever.</p><p>To their rescue has come Peters, who is even surprising those closest to him with his latest surge.</p><p>“She's seen me through my whole minor-league career and yeah, I've never done that before,” Peters said of his wife, Erin. “She was surprised.”</p><p>As recently as the last week of spring training, Tristan and Erin thought they could be living in Charlotte this year, uncertain if Peters would break camp with the major league club or be assigned to Triple-A. Now, Peters knows that slumps, or any notion that he’s anything less than an impact player on an AL Central-leading White Sox team, are just temporary.</p><p>“Those stretches are always frustrating and tough, because you think all these thoughts that aren’t true about yourself,” Peters told the Sun-Times. “But I’ve done it before, and I can do it again.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Jonathan Cannon returns to taxed White Sox pitching staff, touting an overhauled arsenal
entries.summary: <p>Back in 2024, <b>Jonathan Cannon</b>’s rookie-year emergence was a note of encouragement in a White Sox season that offered few others. In Sox pitching circles, comparisons to Giants’ sinkerballing ace Logan Webb were once invoked.</p><p>Instead, Cannon ran up a 5.82 ERA in 2025 and lost his rotation spot, and has spent almost all of this season at Triple-A Charlotte. His return to Chicago is mostly about an injury to <b>Huascar Brazoban</b>, and a pitching staff that's logged 16 games in 16 days, further exhausted by <b>Sean Burke</b> lasting just three innings Wednesday due to a career-high eight walks</p><p>“These guys are running on fumes,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b>.</p><p>But buried underneath both a poor start and the cozy, hitting-friendly environs of the Charlotte Knights’ home park, Cannon has overhauled his approach. He’s abandoned chasing grounders with multiple sinker types that were failing to deliver them, in favor of a four-seam fastball that’s carried him to a 4.13 ERA and a 23.8% strikeout rate over his last 12 outings.</p><p>“I didn't throw my four-seam at all hardly in ‘24 when I came up, but it performed really well,” Cannon told the Sun-Times. “It was just what the hitters were telling us. The more I used it, the results were really good and were consistent. I really feel the four-seam brings a lot more swing-and-miss into my arsenal. Especially if I’m pitching a little bit out of the bullpen here, that’s going to be very beneficial, and it sets up my other pitches a lot as well.”</p><p>Sinking the baseball from a low three-quarters arm slot comes naturally to Cannon, to a fault. All his other pitches also move downward, and elevated four-seamers have filled a void in his arsenal for something to change the eye-level of opposing hitters. It might not be enough to get Cannon’s rotation spot anytime soon, but with the Sox’ current quest for starters, a foot in the door could be worth plenty.</p><p><b>Burger back in town</b></p><p>Three years ago, an ill-fated trade sending <b>Jake Burger</b> to the Marlins for left-hander <b>Jake Eder</b> proved to be the final major move before the <b>Ken Williams</b> and <b>Rick Hahn</b>-led front office was purged, and the Sox hurdled toward three-straight 100-loss seasons.</p><p>Returning this week with the Rangers marks the first time the former Sox first-round pick has seen his old stomping grounds energized by meaningful baseball since departing.</p><p>“I love coming back to the city, and there's a lot of fond memories in this ballpark,” Burger said. “They have a good team, and these are always fun games when you're playing a first-place team versus another first-place team.”</p><p>Burger speaks warmly of general manager <b>Chris Getz</b>, who was the Sox farm director as he battled back from multiple Achilles tears and two seasons entirely lost to injury, to have a major league career with 111 home runs and counting. That includes two this week against his old club, which produced some enjoyable chirping.</p><p>“It’s always good fun. This is always a place where the fans are going to give it to you, no matter who you are.”</p><p><b>Martin on rehab</b></p><p><b>Davis Martin</b> will make a rehab start with Triple-A Charlotte on Thursday, which could line him up to rejoin the White Sox rotation next week if it goes well. <b>Kyle Teel</b> caught for the first time in his Knights rehab assignment on Wednesday.</p><p><b>Peters makes it five</b></p><p>With a fifth-inning two-run shot to right on Wednesday night, <b>Tristan Peters</b> tied the Sox' franchise record with home runs in five consecutive games. He's the eighth Sox hitter to accomplish the feat, including <b>Munetaka Murakami</b> this April.<br></p>

entries.title: First Illinois lawsuit linked to Cyclospora outbreak filed by Chicago librarian
entries.summary: <p>A Chicago librarian who was sickened after eating Taco Bell have filed apparently the first Illinois lawsuit linked to the Cyclospora outbreak, officials, their law firm announced Thursday morning. </p><p>Alonso Zaragoza and Jadhira Sanchez, husband and wife, of Chicago, sued Taylor Fresh Foods, Inc. and Taylor Farms California, Inc. alleging that the shredded iceberg lettuce those companies grew, processed and distributed carried Cyclospora cayetanensis. </p><p>Sanchez did not get sick.</p><p>The complaint, filed Aug. 21, includes counts of strict product liability, breach of express and implied warranty, negligence, and loss of consortium against each company, according to a statement from Marler Clark, a law firm representing the plaintiffs. </p><p>The complaint notes that on July 11, Zaragoza ordered a Chalupa Supreme box meal at a Northwest Side Taco Bell that contained fresh shredded iceberg lettuce and after eating it, he felt symptoms related to Cyclospora that increased in severity over the span of several days. </p><p>By about noon on July 13, he had become sweaty, feverish, and dizzy, and he was forced to lie down in the basement of the library where he works before leaving early and returning home, according to the complaint. The next day, he was unable to work. </p><p>On July 15, Zaragoza, a librarian, went to the emergency room at Northwestern Memorial Hospital for intravenous fluids and was discharged the next afternoon, according to the statement.</p><p>The Food and Drug Administration announced its investigation of shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell the day Zaragoza was discharged and named Taylor Farms de Mexico the day after, the law firm said. </p><p>But Zaragoza wasn't tested for a parasite until his third clinic visit on July 26 and the positive test result came back Aug. 4, according to the complaint. </p><p>"Alonso Zaragoza did everything a person is supposed to do," his attorneys said in the statement. "He worked until he could not stand up, went to an emergency room, went back for care twice more, and it was still August 4 before anybody could tell him what he had."</p><p>Sanchez is suing for losses related to how the Cyclospora impacted Zaragoza, including a lack of sleep for the first five days of his symptoms, an altered, nearly all-liquid household diet to accomodate Zaragoza's needs and time away from work and personal obligations to care for him. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/07/14/illinois-reports-216-cases-of-diarrhea-inducing-cyclosporiasis" target="_blank" >Cyclosporiasis</a> is an intestinal illness caused by the microscopic parasite cyclospora. Infection often comes after eating fresh fruits and vegetables and can lead to watery diarrhea, stomach cramps, gas and nausea.</p><p>Taylor Fresh Foods, a California-based farm and food company, on July 17 voluntarily recalled iceberg salad and shredded lettuce products distributed in 27 states, including Illinois.</p><p>The voluntary recall came after the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cdc.gov/cyclosporiasis/outbreaks/07-26/index.html" target="_blank" >CDC</a> identified shredded lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Michigan, Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia as a source of widespread outbreaks in those states. Taco Bell removed the affected lettuce from its supply chain across the country and planned to replace it in select states, the company previously said.</p><p>Zaragoza wasn’t immediately available for comment. </p>

entries.title: Roger Goodell: NFL wants to make sure Illinois has 'opportunity' to keep Bears
entries.summary:
NFL commissioner Roger Goodell confirmed Wednesday that he recently met with Illinois officials about a potential Bears stadium.

“We want to make sure that Arlington Heights and Illinois have an opportunity, and Indiana as well, to put their best foot forward,” he told reporters at the NFL’s quarterly meeting.

He claimed the commissioner’s office is often involved in stadium politicking.

“I’m involved in a lot of stadium efforts,” he said, per USA Today. “It’s not unusual for me to be involved in conversations with either public officials or others. Or our staff. These are important decisions, not just for the communities but for teams and the NFL.”

The Bears are studying two potential stadium sites in Hammond, Ind., for a domed stadium but have yet to rule out building in Illinois altogether. They own 326 acres in Arlington Heights, where they have tried to push for property tax breaks, but to no avail.

The Bears pushed for PILOT legislation, which would have allowed them to negotiate payments in lieu of taxes, but that plan died at the end of the spring session. The House adjourned without voting on a last-minute option that would have allowed any Cook County municipality with more than 70,000 residents to create their own stadium financing authority.

Barring a special session to take up the Bears’ cause, lawmakers won’t return for their next session until the fall.

The Bears’ board of directors voted in early June to focus on their Indiana plan, for which they’ve pledged $2 billion. Bears president/CEO Kevin Warren and chairman George McCaskey didn’t rule out Illinois earlier this month.

Goodell did not give a timeline for the Bears making a decision. Their stadium search has dragged on for more than five years.

times for service to be restored. NIPSCO reported more than 60% of its customers — roughly 370,000 — lost power during the storm and aftermath. Gary suffered the most "extensive and complex damage," a company executive said.</p><p><b>In their words</b>: Once power was mostly restored, we spoke with residents Wednesday about their experiences and recovery.</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>Allison Looney, local volunteer</b>:</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center">"[We were without power for] 13 days. ... I have never been that long without power or internet. The experience [was] stressful, extremely stressful, very hot and muggy and dark. ... We lost all our food. .. It was pretty intense. A tree came down, actually hit my roof, hit my car, and then landed on my porch."</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>Isaac Mootye, executive director of Brother’s Keeper shelter</b>:</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center">"We lost power here in the shelter for over a week. So obviously, you got 25 men in the dark, which is pretty dangerous because these guys are homeless and a lot of them have come from sordid backgrounds. And then, we have people here who are accountants, doctors, nurses — people who are down on their luck — and they come here for a bridge over troubled waters."</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center"><b>Miles Lewis, local volunteer</b>:</p><p class="cms-textAlign-center">"We are strong, we are fighters, we are resilient, and we are brilliant. I'm going to tell you that the people of Gary, we mind our own business, we keep to ourselves, and we are a strong people. You think the world has forgotten about us, but we don't forget about the world. And we know how to stand together and come together as a community."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbuhjk-l-n/" target="_blank" ><b>READ Smyth can't exist without its burger-forward sister restaurant downstairs, The Loyalist, and vice versa.</p><p><b>Anniversary accolades</b>: Smyth is celebrating 10 years in business this month, a decade marked by recognitions, including three Michelin stars and being dubbed the No. 1 restaurant in North America in May by 50 Best.</p><p><b>How they do it</b>: The success of the Shields' restaurants, much like their romantic relationship, is built on a strong foundation of friendship, creativity and teamwork. href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbuhjk-l-tu/" target="_blank" >Mendy Kong</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbuhjk-l-il/" target="_blank" >Minju But the group's fans have kept the fire burning during that time.</p><p>Earlier this month, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbuhjk-l-ir/" target="_blank" >Gov. JB Pritzker declared Aug. 27 and 28 “BTS Day” in Illinois</a> after petitioning by Chicago BTS Army and the HANA Center, an immigrant advocacy nonprofit in Irving Park.</p><p>And ahead of BTS' return to Chicago this week, fans have been gathering to bond over their shared love of the K-pop titans, including a trivia night at Lincoln Park's Replay on Tuesday.</p><p>Between the arcade games in Replay, the tables and bar were packed with buzzing BTS fans ahead of the South Korean superstars' sold-out "Arirang" world tour shows Thursday and Friday at Soldier Field. Many eventgoers were no strangers to local events hosted by fellow fans, and relished the friendships they were able to make through attending.</p><p>"By being a fan, I was able to connect with other people that I might never have met if I didn’t know [BTS], and those people became my best friends," said Megan Herrera, 25, of Pilsen.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbuhjk-l-iy/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>Today's daily question is inspired by a segment on <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydbuhjk-l-ij/" target="_blank" >WBEZ’s “Say More” call-in show</a>.</p><p>From cyclospora in lettuce to salmonella in jalapeños, <b>how are you handling food recalls this summer?</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). entries.title: FCC's Carr's vendetta against ABC rooted in Trump's personal grievances
entries.summary: <p>Last April, the Federal Communications Commission <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/04/28/trump-administrations-review-of-abcs-broadcast-licenses-looks-like-illegal-jawboning/" target="_blank" >announced</a> that it was reviewing the broadcast licenses held by ABC's eight network-owned TV stations years before they were scheduled for renewal. The FCC had not conducted an early review of any broadcast license in more than half a century, and it had never done so simultaneously for all the stations operated by a particular network.</p><p>That unprecedented action, ABC and its parent company, Disney, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/08/18/disney-sues-fcc-for-retaliatory-investigation-of-abc/" target="_blank" >argue</a> in a federal <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.dcd.295648/gov.uscourts.dcd.295648.1.0_1.pdf" target="_blank" >lawsuit</a> filed last week, is part of an unconstitutional <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/22/trumps-threats-to-yank-broadcast-licenses-are-part-of-a-speech-chilling-intimidation-campaign/" target="_blank" >intimidation campaign</a> that has already had a chilling impact on broadcast journalism. A bipartisan group of former FCC officials, including commissioners appointed by Ronald Reagan and George H.W. Bush, <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/KXZ8-5CAH" target="_blank" >agrees</a> that the agency has launched "an assault on free speech disguised as regulatory process" to "punish speech disfavored by the Trump administration."</p><p>President Donald Trump has been <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/18/how-the-fcc-became-the-speech-police/" target="_blank" >threatening</a> to yank the licenses of broadcasters who irk him since his first term. But this time around, the FCC's Trump-appointed chairman, Brendan Carr, seems eager to act on that vindictive impulse.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fb0000" name="module-fb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Carr <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/04/01/fcc-chair-investigates-disney-over-potential-past-and-present-dei-policies/" target="_blank" >portrays</a> the ABC review as a response to "diversity, equity, and inclusion" programs that may qualify as "unlawful discrimination." But he has <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/N3SQ-QX3G" target="_blank" >made it clear</a> that the FCC also is considering the broader question of whether ABC's stations are serving "the public interest," a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/09/23/brendan-carr-says-networks-must-serve-the-public-interest-what-does-that-mean/" target="_blank" >vague statutory mandate</a> that he views as a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/23/brendan-carr-says-abcs-refusal-to-air-a-trump-speech-could-affect-renewal-of-its-broadcast-licenses/" target="_blank" >license</a> to override freedom of the press.</p><p>The president's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/11/19/a-reporters-unwelcome-questions-provoke-yet-another-trump-threat-to-yank-broadcast-licenses/" target="_blank" >beef</a> with ABC includes <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/C48H-XQEP" target="_blank" >news coverage</a> he views as <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/4DMG-KKG8" target="_blank" >overwhelmingly negative</a>, its fact-checking during a 2024 <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/VP84-VE6W" target="_blank" >presidential debate</a>, anti-Trump commentary on shows such as <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/23/the-fcc-wants-to-police-how-many-conservatives-appear-on-the-view/" target="_blank" >“The View”</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/09/25/fcc-threats-against-jimmy-kimmel-echo-a-century-of-speech-control/" target="_blank" >“Jimmy Kimmel Live”</a> and the network's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/17/trump-threatens-to-revoke-abc-and-nbc-licenses-for-not-broadcasting-his-election-speech/" target="_blank" >refusal</a> to air his July 16 primetime speech, which followed a long line of similar calls by TV networks under prior administrations. Carr, who routinely <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/LA8K-L24L" target="_blank" >amplifies</a> such complaints, <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/BW6P-5QN9" target="_blank" >agrees</a> that they demand the FCC's attention.</p><p>Shortly after taking office, Carr <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/02/05/how-the-fccs-warrior-for-free-speech-became-our-censor-in-chief/" target="_blank" >reopened</a> an FCC investigation of ABC's allegedly biased debate moderation. Last September, Carr <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/09/18/brendan-carr-flagrantly-abused-his-powers-to-cancel-jimmy-kimmel/" target="_blank" >threatened</a> ABC stations with fines or license revocation if they failed to punish Kimmel for suggesting that conservative activist Charlie Kirk's assassin was a Trump supporter.</p><p>Carr, who announced the early review of ABC's licenses the day after Trump and his wife objected to a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/06/trumps-responses-to-kimmel-and-comey-highlight-his-disregard-for-freedom-of-speech/" target="_blank" >joke</a> Kimmel had made on his show, <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/23/brendan-carr-says-abcs-refusal-to-air-a-trump-speech-could-affect-renewal-of-its-broadcast-licenses/" target="_blank" >says</a> the network's decision against broadcasting Trump's speech will figure in that process, which could drag on for years. Carr also has <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/11/brendan-carrs-equal-time-threat-against-the-view-is-blatantly-unconstitutional-abc-says/" target="_blank" >threatened</a> to rescind  the long-standing "bona fide news exemption" of "The View" from the FCC's "equal time" rule, which in practice would amount to a ban on interviews with political candidates.</p><p>Such regulatory threats have an observable impact. ABC and its affiliates immediately met Carr's demands by suspending Kimmel's show for a week last fall, "The View" has stopped interviewing political candidates, and ABC says it carried Trump's whole speech on its streaming channel only because it was worried about antagonizing the FCC.</p><p>The effects extend beyond ABC. Once TV networks understand that the FCC's objections to their reporting or editorial judgments can pose an existential threat to the stations they operate, they are apt to think twice before making decisions that might upset the president.</p><p>From Carr's perspective, that is the whole point. "Through this proceeding," the former FCC officials <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/KXZ8-5CAH" target="_blank" >say</a>, the commission "seeks to censor Disney's and ABC's speech and send a chilling message to all broadcasters: Carry speech we don't like at your peril."</p><p>Carr, an <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/02/05/how-the-fccs-warrior-for-free-speech-became-our-censor-in-chief/" target="_blank" >avowed</a> First Amendment champion, improbably <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/blogs/politico-press/2026/07/31/full-transcript-chairman-of-the-federal-communications-commission-brendan-carr-01020589" target="_blank" >claims</a> he is trying to "re-empower local TV stations" by "reminding them" about their "unique public interest obligations." It is hard to see how threatening to put broadcasters out of business empowers them to do anything but kowtow to the president.</p><p>"It's not our role to be the speech police," Carr <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/blogs/politico-press/2026/07/31/full-transcript-chairman-of-the-federal-communications-commission-brendan-carr-01020589" target="_blank" >told</a> Politico last month. Yet Carr, who <a class="Link" href="https://perma.cc/2PYM-7RA4" target="_blank" >brags</a> that Trump is "winning" his fight against "the fake news media," clearly <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/BrendanCarrFCC/status/1902414297327599842" target="_blank" >sees himself</a> as a warrior in that battle, which conflates "the public interest" with the president's personal grievances.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c90000" name="module-c90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Tariffs, bullying behavior have Canadians rightfully trashing Trump
entries.summary: <p>This summer, America played host to one of the biggest international events on the planet, the World Cup, drawing millions of foreigners to our cities and towns, our stadiums and our national parks, where many of them had never been before.</p><p>The consensus was, America is awesome — visitors from Bolivia, Scotland, Uzbekistan and everywhere in between marveled at the sheer size of our great nation, the diversity of our topography, the deliciousness of our foodstuffs and, perhaps most importantly, the kindness of our people. (Not to mention, our eighth wonder of the world — Buc-ee’s.)</p><p>What a difference a month makes.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-5c0000" name="module-5c0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Despite our friends in far-flung places singing our praises, now, to hear our closest neighbors tell it, America is nothing but a “ <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/antoniopequenoiv/2026/08/24/canadas-doug-ford-calls-trump-a-dictator-as-economic-war-escalates/" target="_blank" >bully</a>” and a “ <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/08/24/trumps-trade-war-with-canada-has-carney-facing-his-biggest-test-yet/" target="_blank" >thug</a>.”</p><p>After trade negotiations with Canada collapsed this week, and President Donald Trump announced a whopping 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods — including Canadian whiskey and hockey sticks — it’s no surprise our friends to the north are less than pleased with their downstairs neighbors.</p><p>In our defense, not all of us are responsible for electing the bully and thug in question — and if <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trumps-approval-holds-record-low-us-support-iran-war-falls-reuters-ipsos-poll-2026-08-24/" target="_blank" >polls</a> are any indication, most Americans agree with Canada that Trump is doing a terrible job. But still, it’s hard to hear.</p><p>Especially since we love Canadians, and we very much want them to love us back.</p><p>But after spending years threatening to invade Canada and make it the “51st state,” and mocking its leaders with petty nicknames and schoolyard insults, Trump may have finally put Canadians’ famous politeness to the test.</p><p>“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2026/08/24/trumps-trade-war-with-canada-has-carney-facing-his-biggest-test-yet/" target="_blank" >said</a> Prime Minister Mark Carney. “We’re going to hit back.”</p><p>Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew <a class="Link" href="https://www.wjtv.com/news/business/ap-quebecs-premier-says-canada-us-trade-talks-are-far-from-over/" target="_blank" >called</a> Trump “erratic,” “irresponsible” and “a bad person” who was “not to be trusted.”</p><p>And Ontario Premier Doug Ford wasn’t nearly as nice, <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/antoniopequenoiv/2026/08/24/canadas-doug-ford-calls-trump-a-dictator-as-economic-war-escalates/" target="_blank" >calling</a> Trump the “king of bankruptcies,” and telling him to “Kiss my ass.”</p><p>Again, these are our friends talking!</p><p>But their righteous indignation is justified — we are in the midst of an unpopular war that we can’t seem to end, our economy is in the toilet, we’re banning books, deporting children with cancer, shooting unarmed protesters, spreading measles and covering up for one of our most notorious sex offenders. And we have the audacity to attack our nice and normal friends?</p><p>But it’s not just an issue of bad manners. Americans have long been accused of that.</p><p>It may be an election issue now.</p><p>States like Michigan, Maine, Alaska and Ohio, all of which border Canada and are important trade partners, also have another thing in common: highly competitive Senate races.</p><p>And despite all but Maine voting for Trump in the last election, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings/senate-race-ratings" target="_blank" >Cook Political Report</a> lists all four as a toss-up.</p><p>The Canada trade issue is real to these voters; for autoworkers in Michigan who rely on Canadian aluminum and steel; for 95% of Mainers who rely on Canada for home heating; for Ohioans who use Canadian metals and machinery; for Alaskans who need Canadian crude.</p><p>So Democratic Senate candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Mary Peltola in Alaska have yet another important talking point to add to their reservoirs — that Trump’s dumb trade war, much like his dumb actual war, is going to make voters’ lives worse.</p><p>Add it to the pile — a <a class="Link" href="https://www.ft.com/content/fd40a98d-2a7f-4246-a296-73e956bf03c0?syn-25a6b1a6=1" target="_blank" >majority of voters</a> already believe they are worse off under Trump, and this won’t help.</p><p>With fewer than 70 days until the midterm elections, the imprudence of picking a fight with important allies — who now seem prepared to unleash retaliatory economic pain on Americans in competitive states hardly seems debatable.</p><p>But Trump seems hell bent on totally destroying whatever good will we still had left on the world stage.</p><p>Talk about an own goal.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-390000" name="module-390000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Questions and answers: 5 certainties, uncertainties for the Bears heading into 2026 season
entries.summary: <p>There are no guarantees in the NFL, and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> have gotten a harsh reminder of that from the rash of injuries they’ve dealt with in training camp.</p><p>But to whatever extent a team can count on something, there’s a lot to like about what they have going into this season. There also is quite a bit about which to be skeptical. Their success hinges on their strengths turning out to be exactly that and their hopes materializing.</p><p>Here are five things they can reasonably bank on this season:</p><p><b>Loveland being unstoppable</b></p><p>Tight end Colston Loveland was a surprising pick by the Bears at No. 10 overall, but now it makes total sense. He’s too fast for linebackers and too big for defensive backs, and he’s caught virtually everything Caleb Williams has thrown him. While coach Ben Johnson wants to spread the ball around, it’ll be going to Loveland the most.</p><p><b>Johnson being himself</b></p><p>There’s cause for worry anytime a player comes off a major injury, but Jaylon Johnson seems back to normal after missing most of last season because of core-muscle surgery. He’s been one of the most rock-solid Bears of the past decade, was at his peak as a shutdown corner before he got hurt and is still just 27. The Bears will face many elite receivers, and it’s luxury to solve that issue simply by sticking Johnson on them.</p><p><b>Swift getting it done</b></p><p>Running back <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/01/02/bears-rb-dandre-swift-adapted-to-new-scheme-hard-coaching-and-is-delivering-best-season-of-career" >D’Andre Swift</a> is coming off a great season thanks largely to how receptive he was to coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> and former running backs coach Eric Bieniemy. He maintained his big-play capability while becoming a reliable north-south runner. That brought out the best of him and will get him paid, and Swift is sticking with that approach.</p><p><b>The Ben Factor</b></p><p>Ben Johnson changed everything when he walked into Halas Hall. Standards were raised. Practices became more physical. Work ethic was redefined. For all the possible flaws in this roster and all the hope being put in young players reaching their potential, Johnson brings credibility to the equation. There’s a belief inside the building that he’ll get the absolute most out of this team.</p><p><b>Williams delivering incredible moments</b></p><p>Williams won everyone over with his heroics last season: His overtime touchdown pass to beat the Packers in the regular season, the fourth-and-eight jump pass against them in the playoffs and his stunning fourth-down heave to force overtime against the Rams in the divisional round. Those were unforgettable, and there are more coming.</p><p>And here are five areas that are uncertain until proven otherwise:</p><p><b>Williams being a clockwork passer</b></p><p>Among the things Bears coaches have stressed to him this offseason is that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/05/22/bears-coaches-have-a-simple-message-to-qb-caleb-williams-this-offseason-do-less" >making a bunch of relatively easy plays in the first three quarters could set the team up to coast in the fourth</a>. Johnson is excited about Williams’ improv skills and is looking to enhance them, but he also needs Williams to be a technician when it comes to the basics, and that’s not something he showed consistently his first two seasons.</p><p><b>Pass rush being enough</b></p><p>The Bears keep saying improvement in their pass rush will come from within, but they don’t have anything concrete to back that up. They have a legitimate No. 1 defensive end in Montez Sweat, but everyone else needs to show something: Dayo Odeyingbo has four sacks in his last 28 games, Austin Booker has six career sacks and Shemar Turner is still on the physically unable-to-perform list.</p><p><b>Getting left tackle right</b></p><p>Here’s what Ben Johnson said about left tackle just this week: “I don’t know that we are 100% sold on who that guy is going to be.” Yikes. Again? Braxton Jones likely will be the starter Week 1 against the Panthers, but that didn’t last long last season. Johnson won’t hesitate to try Theo Benedet, and the big-picture hope is that Ozzy Trapilo eventually comes back.</p><p><b>Odunze breaking through</b></p><p>Wide receiver Rome Odunze has been good, but a player drafted ninth overall needs to be great. Two receivers drafted after him have posted more yards, and three have more catches. Odunze has said multiple times he hasn’t done enough yet. He has looked strong in training camp coming off a stress fracture in his foot, but few players on the team have more to prove this season.</p><p><b>Taking the North</b></p><p>The Bears can’t expect to have so much cushion in the NFC North. Last season, they led the division most of the season despite going 2-4 in it and benefited from the Packers’ late-season slide, some hiccups by the Lions and the Vikings’ quarterback mess. All three of those teams have great coaches, and none of them are going to stay down.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Dear Abby: Visiting niece starts smear campaign against her dad
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I got permission from my estranged brother to invite his 17-year-old daughter, "Ella," to spend a month with my family this summer. We live on the East Coast, and she lives on the West Coast.</p><p>Ella is about to graduate from high school and has had a difficult home life and relationship with her dad and stepmother. After making her travel arrangements, I came across recent social media posts that my niece wrote disparaging her father. I'm in no position to discipline or judge her, but I felt that I had to say something so she knows that I don't condone what she has done.</p><p>I'm now second-guessing whether it's a good idea to have Ella around my 13- and 9-year-old children this summer. I told her the following: "I hadn't seen your post about your father and stepmother. As a loving adult, I want you to know I think it's very inappropriate. These kinds of postings tend to reflect more about the person posting than the people the post is about. For your own good, you should know that you, too, may be judged for what you have done — if not now, possibly in the future when you least want or expect it."</p><p>Ella didn't respond to me and continues to write more disrespectful posts. Should I say anything more? I don't think my brother knows about the posts, though my niece complained online about his having "hacked" her accounts. — <i>HAVING SECOND THOUGHTS</i></p><p><b>DEAR SECOND THOUGHTS:</b> I wish you had mentioned the reason for your estrangement from your brother. Contact him and ask if he is aware of the comments Ella has posted and continues to post. If he is unaware, you should alert him. The choice of whether to cancel your niece's visit is up to you, but from where I sit, she appears to be an unhappy girl who could use a break from Dad.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 63-year-old woman who retired about eight years ago. I have decided to go back into the workforce — nothing huge, just a job to enable me to keep up with rising costs and to set some money aside. My problem is that everyone wants you to apply online.</p><p>I go online to look for work, I find something of interest, I click on it, and it takes me to a sign-in page for some sort of job site (such as Monster or Indeed). I fill out my information, and then I get a whole list of jobs, none of which are the one I originally clicked on. I have never had this much trouble finding a job. Any advice would be welcome. I am running out of options. — <i>WILLING TO WORK</i></p><p><b>DEAR WILLING TO WORK:</b> Applying through those online job sites can feel like talking to a wall. Since you aren't looking for anything fancy, the old-fashioned approach may work better. Check the bulletin boards of community centers, senior centers, local colleges, libraries and similar establishments. When you are out and about, keep your eyes peeled for "help wanted" notices. If you find yourself near a place you'd like to work, it can't hurt to stop in and ask if they need help. Also, don't forget the classified ads in your local newspaper!</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned the column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Ranking the NFL's 8 new alternate uniforms
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> weren’t the only team to release an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/25/bears-new-nike-rivalry-uniform-unveil-christmas-day-packers-2026" target="_blank" >alternate uniform</a> this week. Seven other teams did the same, with mixed results.</p><p>The Sun-Times’ Patrick Finley and Brian Sandalow agreed on the best two and the worst three; in between, Finley preferred the Bears, and Sandalow the Packers and Titans. After a vote, here's how they ranked the “Rivalries” uniforms of all eight teams, from the near-perfect to the embarrassing:<br> </p><h3>1. VIKINGS</h3><p>SANDALOW: A mark of a good alternate uniform is one that could be the basis for a full redesign. That’s what the Vikings accomplished.</p><p>Using a deeper purple, gold instead of yellow and a “Nordic knot” pattern for the helmet, pants and sleeve striping, Minnesota found a way to thread the needle of something new and fresh with something that’s related to the team’s traditional identity. There is the usual and unnecessary Nike flair – on the front helmet bumper, Minnesota’s SKOL chant is translated in characters from the Rune system once used in Scandinavia – but that’s a minor demerit and won’t be visible on TV.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">This palette 🎨 <a href="https://t.co/bfBYmD1TGd">pic.twitter.com/bfBYmD1TGd</a></p>— Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) <a href="https://x.com/Vikings/status/2092666228523274511?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 26, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Vikings’ standard home and road uniforms are already solid, but if they decided to go with these and a white version, they’d actually be upgrading. That’s how well the Vikings did here.<br> </p><h3>2. TEXANS</h3><p>FINLEY: The NFL’s youngest team doesn’t have to bow to tradition. The result is a fun, shiny, candy-coated set that stands feels, well, joyful. Alternate uniforms are supposed to be fun, right?</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Trunks pop. Tops drop. <a href="https://t.co/koAFxpjmJ5">pic.twitter.com/koAFxpjmJ5</a></p>— Houston Texans (@HoustonTexans) <a href="https://x.com/HoustonTexans/status/2092323468045942930?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Texans’ numbers are based on the iconic “Be Someone” graffiti on a Houston bridge. The sleeve tiles, helmet stripe and player names are in a lighter blue that pay homage to the blue street tiles in the city itself.  White helmets are lazy. But the Old English “H” that the team debuted on a navy helmet two years ago pops on their white hats.</p><p>None of that storytelling matters unless the uniforms look good, though. And these do.<br> </p><h3>3. PACKERS</h3><p>SANDALOW: The good news is that the Packers kept the same basic striping from their usual set. Elements match and come together to make a coherent uniform.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">For our history. For our future. For you. <a href="https://t.co/a2cVbuLlhE">pic.twitter.com/a2cVbuLlhE</a></p>— Green Bay Packers (@packers) <a href="https://x.com/packers/status/2092252322092990664?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The bad news is all the storytelling they need. The vintage green and off white are meant to evoke historic Packers stock certificates. The numbers have an engraved treatment reminiscent of lettering on paper currency to honor the “financial contributions from the fans that helped sustain the franchise over the years.” Yes, really.</p><p>The best thing about traditional uniforms is how little artificial marketing copy they need. The colors and design speak for themselves thanks to decades of memories and moments. It’s jarring to read through this stuff for a team like the Packers or Bears, even if the end product is passable like Green Bay’s.<br> </p><h3>4. BEARS</h3><p>SANDALOW: This uniform is a mishmash of ideas that doesn’t really come together. So, if the Bears were trying to mimic most of their history, they succeeded.</p><p>Nothing matches. The orange helmet is not new, albeit with a different front bumper and obligatory Chicago stars on the rear padding. For whatever reason, the Bears chose the number font from 1948 – a team that won nothing – to go on a jersey with today’s sleeve stripes but turned 90 degrees to echo the 1920s style. The original 1983 </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Inspired by the past. Built for the future. <a href="https://t.co/WzxAIyzOcA">pic.twitter.com/WzxAIyzOcA</a></p>— Chicago Bears (@ChicagoBears) <a href="https://x.com/ChicagoBears/status/2092251959818359056?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>George Halas tribute patch is above the heart, which is a nice touch but doesn’t go with anything else.</p><p>The pants – orange with a blue-white-blue stripe – and 1940s-style orange-striped navy socks don’t complement each other. It’s like the Bears decided to throw as much navy and orange at a wall to see what stuck. Not much did.<br> </p><h3>5. TITANS</h3><p>FINLEY: The Titans continue to lean into the Houston Oilers’ baby blue palette — and it remains an odd troll job for a franchise that moved to Tennessee in 1997.</p><p>I was a fan of the six-string accent they used in remodeling their standard uniforms a few months ago, and I’m thrilled that they put it on the sleeve and light blue helmet here.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">What do you think, Titans fans? <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/TitanUp?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#TitanUp</a> <a href="https://t.co/nkq4CIcpMc">pic.twitter.com/nkq4CIcpMc</a></p>— Tennessee Titans (@Titans) <a href="https://x.com/Titans/status/2092259806316777785?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The “Music City” moniker works — it’s a lot better than “Bold City,” which we’ll get to later — and the neon numbers would be home on Lower Broadway.<br> </p><h3>6. COLTS</h3><p>FINLEY: These poor Colts. Unlike their AFC South brethren, they have a real history to respect. And unlike almost any other team in the NFL, they have only one team color — blue — with no accents to play off of.</p><p>Come design time, then, they don’t have many places to turn. Their “Indiana Nights” set unveiled in 2023 — are Indiana nights something to aspire to? — paired a heather blue jersey with a black helmet. Their “Rivalries” uniform is slate gray — they claim it echoes an anvil — with a blue helmet.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="zxx" dir="ltr"><a href="https://t.co/gXrYxcvapT">pic.twitter.com/gXrYxcvapT</a></p>— Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) <a href="https://x.com/Colts/status/2092253976888578522?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>They look like the University of Kentucky. That’s not a compliment.<br> </p><h3>7. JAGUARS</h3><h3></h3><p>FINLEY: The Jaguars’ “Bold City” uniforms are as bold as the city of Jacksonville itself. Which is to say, they’re not.</p><p>It’s a white jersey with black numbers that look like old-school curvy UCLA numbers — without the color or charm — and a cursive “Jaguars” written above them. The best thing about the Jaguars is their throwback teal shade. Why wear black and white?</p><p>The black pants have a chance to actually be daring — there are sublimated jaguar spots — but I’ll be curious to see if they show well on the field or if they’ll look like Peg Bundy from “Married With Children.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Fortune favors us.<a href="https://x.com/hashtag/DUUUVAL?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#DUUUVAL</a> <a href="https://t.co/Fdy8vVYjgw">pic.twitter.com/Fdy8vVYjgw</a></p>— Jacksonville Jaguars (@Jaguars) <a href="https://x.com/Jaguars/status/2092251334523457747?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Jaguars’ “Duuuval!”cheer is silly and fun — it’s the name of the county — and something they should have leaned into for a jersey.<br> </p><h3>8. LIONS</h3><p>SANDALOW: Are we sure these weren’t designed for the Panthers instead of the Lions? Seriously, how did Nike and the Lions not bring in fresh eyes to look at these before they were finalized?</p><p>No, these are not a dead ringer for Carolina, but there’s enough of a resemblance to make you stop. The shame of these is that the Lions have a rich history to draw from, and they play in a vibrant and important American city which should offer more than enough inspiration for designers. Instead, this is a Lions-Panthers-Jets (pre-rebrand) hybrid.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Defend. The. entries.title: Fall movies 2026: Richard Roeper’s 12 most anticipated
entries.summary: <p>Talk about a tough act to follow.</p><p>The summer of 2026 has been a historic one for the movies on multiple fronts. Christopher Nolan’s groundbreaking epic “The Odyssey” has crossed the $1.1 billion mark worldwide, as fans made pilgrimages to screens with IMAX 70mm film capabilities, and theaters scheduling showings in the middle of the night to keep up with demand. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” and “Toy Story 5” were massive hits as well. Meanwhile, the low-budget psychological horror film “Obsession” enjoyed a sensational run and became the ultimate summer sleeper hit, actually earning more on each of the first three weekends of June than it did when it opened in late spring.</p><p>We’re not going to see the same level of box-office success for the fall season, defined as films released from Labor Day weekend through Thanksgiving. Still, there’s no shortage of major sequels and prequels, star-powered vehicles and intriguing smaller films.</p><p><b>Here are my most anticipated movies for fall 2026:</b></p><h3><b>“Practical Magic 2” (September 11)</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-440000" name="image-440000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/44547a2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3216x1805+440+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2F9f%2Fbb225b914bb096c1ccbbecb32cf8%2Fpm2-image-3.jpeg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/afe7b68/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3216x1805+440+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2F9f%2Fbb225b914bb096c1ccbbecb32cf8%2Fpm2-image-3.jpeg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f604426/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3216x1805+440+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fbc%2F9f%2Fbb225b914bb096c1ccbbecb32cf8%2Fpm2-image-3.jpeg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="PM2 - Pictures</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>This is kind of a strange choice for a legacy sequel, given the original in 1998 was neither a critical nor commercial favorite. Still, I’ve got it on the list because the massively talented quartet of Sandra Bullock, Nicole Kidman, Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing are returning, with Joey King and Maisie Williams joining the cast. Perhaps more important, the brilliant Susanne Bier, who has teamed up with Bullock on “Bird Box” and with Kidman for “The Undoing” and “The Perfect Couple,” is directing. Set a quarter-century after the events of the first film, “Practical Magic 2” finds the witchy Owens sisters, played by Bullock and Kidman, embarking on a journey to end the family curse once and for all. Given the director/cast combination here, there’s reason to hope the sequel will surpass the original in quality and box-office performance.</p><hr><p></p><h3><b>“The Weight” (September 18)</b></h3><p>I’m often asked to name my favorite genre of movie and that’s an almost impossible question to answer — but whether it’s a Western or a crime thriller or a character study, I am partial to films that look like they could have been made in the “New Hollywood” era of the 1960s and 1970s, regardless of the time period in which they’re set. (Recent examples would include films such as “Licorice Pizza,” “X,” “The Card Counter” and “Tony.”) It looks like “The Weight” could fill that bill, as it’s reportedly a gritty, historical drama set in 1933, with Ethan Hawke playing an incarcerated man in Oregon who is offered a devil’s bargain by the warden, played by Russell Crowe: smuggle a load of gold through the wilderness and win his freedom. Ethan Hawke is riding a career wave with a series of great performances in challenging roles, and Russell Crowe — well, we <i>know</i> he can play relentless and intimidating.</p><hr><p></p><h3><b>“Resident Evil” (September 18)</b></h3><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a The big-screen treatment of one of Batman’s most notorious enemies is said to be an all-out body horror film, with the title character as the centerpiece of a character-driven psychological tragedy. Tom Rhys Harries plays Matt Hagen, an actor whose life is destroyed after he is disfigured when an affair with a gangster’s girlfriend is discovered. entries.title: After the lights turn on in Gary, the recovery work continues
entries.summary: <p>While much of Northwest Indiana suffered significant power loss from a summer derecho that swept through the region, Gary residents endured some of the longest wait times for service to be restored.</p><p>Utility company NIPSCO reported more than 60% of its customers — roughly 370,000 — lost power during the Aug. 11 storm and subsequent days of severe weather. But Gary suffered the most “extensive and complex damage," a company executive has said. Some residents were left without power for weeks.</p><p>Once power was mostly restored, the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ spoke with five people helping with relief efforts Wednesday about their experiences and how the city is recovering now that lights are back on.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3e0000" name="image-3e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3e19c86/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F12%2F6040017b44a194214ec7e70d903c%2Faftergary-260827-4.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0104d68/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F12%2F6040017b44a194214ec7e70d903c%2Faftergary-260827-4.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/943c58e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7008x3933+0+369/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F7e%2F12%2F6040017b44a194214ec7e70d903c%2Faftergary-260827-4.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Allison Looney, who said she lost power in her home for 13 days, inside Brother’s Keeper where she volunteers in Gary, Ind., Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. We got power on Sunday evening, late. Well, dinner time, about 7 p.m. Our air conditioner kicked on, and our stove was trying to light. So thank God [my husband] was home because he kept hearing a ticking sound like that. So we're thankful that he was home.</p><p>"I have never been that long without power or internet. The experience [was] stressful, extremely stressful, very hot and muggy and dark. It was very dark. We lost all our food. Well, I shouldn't say all of our food. I was able to salvage some of our freezer food. My mom did get power in Crown Point. I was able to cook some there. But it was pretty intense. A tree came down, actually hit my roof, hit my car, and then landed on my porch. entries.title: More than 200 tornadoes have hit Illinois this year. How come?
entries.summary: <p><i>This coverage is made possible through a partnership between WBEZ and </i><a class="Link" href="http://grist.org/" target="_blank" ><i>Grist</i></a><i>, a nonprofit environmental media organization.</i></p><p>So far this year 207 tornadoes and counting have touched down in Illinois. That figure may rise as officials continue working through the remaining post-storm assessments, according to the National Weather Service. The tornado season also has yet to finish, but it has already handily topped the previous record of 142 funnel clouds set just two years ago, according to Trent Ford, the Illinois state climatologist. This is the third year in a row that Illinois has experienced a triple-digit tornado season; the state’s historical average is closer to <a class="Link" href="https://stateclimatologist.isws.illinois.edu/climate-of-illinois/tornadoes-in-illinois/" target="_blank" ><u>50</u></a>.</p><p>“It’s just anything beyond what we would expect,” Ford said.</p><p>The dramatic surge in Illinois and throughout the Midwest contrasts with a decreasing trend of twisters in the Great Plains, the region traditionally billed as Tornado Alley. Experts are still working through the data, trying to understand whether it has been inching eastward, and if so whether climate change has anything to do with it.</p><p>A recent analysis by <a class="Link" href="https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7494372985126957057/" target="_blank" ><u>Steve Nesbitt</u></a>, a meteorologist and professor of atmospheric sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, found that the region is getting a historic hammering. Illinois and Indiana have already recorded the highest level of tornado activity since the National Weather Service started keeping track in 1950. He added that nearby states including Iowa, Missouri, Michigan, and Ohio are in the top 10.</p><p>That said, overall it has been a slow year across the rest of the United States “It has been below average nationally, with the southern Plains and Southeast less active than normal,” Nesbit said.</p><p>Even with the unusual flurry of tornadoes, Illinois remains well short of the all-time record in the U.S. That belongs to Texas, which experienced 255 in 2015. Some experts argue it’s not a fair comparison because Texas is about <a class="Link" href="https://www.mylifeelsewhere.com/state-size-comparison/texas-usa/illinois-usa" target="_blank" ><u>4.7 times</u></a> larger than Illinois. However, Nesbit said that in terms of tornado density, or concentration of tornadoes touching down in 80-kilometer (50 mile) squares, Illinois is on top. He added that as of mid-August no region of the country has had a higher reported density of tornadoes than parts of central Illinois.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Krimberly Guajardo stands among tree branches on her property on the 3600 block Burr St. in Gary, Indiana, Monday, Aug. 17, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>A climate change connection? </h3><p>Tornadoes are the result of atmospheric contrasts and chaos. They develop when moist air near the ground lies beneath drier, hotter air aloft, creating a sandwich of sorts. In this unstable atmosphere, differences in wind speed and direction at different heights create rotation and thunderclouds. “So just a difference between air masses,” said Shel Winkley, chief meteorologist at the research group Climate Central. “That’s also going to provide some spin in the atmosphere.”</p><p>Scientists measure this as “convective available potential energy,” or CAPE, which describes the available fuel for thunderstorm development. Look inside these towering thunderclouds and you’ll find warm air rising but cool air falling, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/about/k-12-education/severe-weather/what-causes-tornadoes" target="_blank" ><u>creates spinning currents</u></a> that can spawn a tornado. One trend scientists can parse, Winkley said, is the increase in the number of potential thunderstorm days. “That doesn’t necessarily mean a tornado will form,” Winkley added, “but we have these higher values of CAPE over the East and the Southeast during the spring than we used to have.”</p><p>The other component is that moisture. An abundantly clear climate signal is playing out in the Gulf of Mexico, which has been <a class="Link" href="https://grist.org/climate/climate-change-supercharge-storm-atmosphere-gulf/" target="_blank" ><u>exceptionally warm of late</u></a>. Since humans began pumping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, the oceans have absorbed more than 90 percent of the additional heat. The hotter the Gulf gets, the more moisture it can pump into the atmosphere, and the more fuel it can provide for thunderstorms and tornadoes. (This is also <a class="Link" href="https://grist.org/extreme-weather/how-climate-change-is-intensifying-hurricanes/" target="_blank" ><u>how climate change is supercharging hurricanes</u></a>, as those storms also love moisture.)</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3b0000"
