class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Neighbors come outside to watch NIPSCO workers address storm damage and downed power lines in Gary, Indiana.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Even given all that, experts agree it doesn’t seem that climate change is in and of itself resulting in more tornadoes. However, on the days when we get the biggest tornado outbreaks, more twisters are touching down, including in Illinois, Winkley said. Tornado Alley also seems to be shifting east, putting new communities in danger, according to Winkley. “At least the science that we have right now, we don’t see a connection between more tornadoes occurring because of climate change,” Winkley said. “It’s more about where they’re occurring, when they’re occurring, and then again the number that they’re happening on specific days versus others.”</p><p>Another wrinkle: It has never been easier to spot a tornado.</p><p>“Our radar data has increased in resolution multiple times over compared to even when I started at this office 20 years ago,” said Ginno Izzi, a senior meteorologist at the National Weather Service office covering Chicago and parts of northwest Indiana. He adds that advancement in radar resolution, satellite data, and remote sensing has made it possible to count smaller tornadoes that might not have been previously detected.</p><p>Better detection has also translated to a better warning system. Izzi’s office, which monitors weather activity in 18 counties in northern and central Illinois, and five counties in northwest Indiana, has issued a record breaking 330 severe thunderstorm and tornado warnings this year.</p><p>Izzi added that despite Illinois’ tornado-heavy year, it’s far too early for any kind of climate change attribution.</p><p>If that seems unsatisfyingly inconclusive, it’s not for lack of trying. Tornadoes are hyperlocal weather events, so they’re difficult to simulate in climate models. Massive hurricanes, on the other hand, are easier to model. So scientists are still working to figure out how much the change in tornado activity is due to natural variability — what you’d expect if humans hadn’t warmed the planet — versus what’s the consequence of runaway greenhouse gas emissions. “That’s still one of those things that we just need faster computers and stronger computers in order to be able to do that sort of modeling with it,” Winkley said, “and we’re just not quite there yet.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/29/what-to-know-tornadoes-chicago-suburbs-wheaton-lansing" >What to know after tornadoes tore through Chicago suburbs</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/03/12/tornadoes-weather-illinois-chicago-suburbs-indiana-hail-storm-flooding" >Are tornadoes surging in Illinois? What you need to know</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Previewing Week 2's top high school football games
entries.summary: <p>It’s a loaded weekend around the area in Week 2. Here are previews of a few of the best games.</p><h3>No. 3 Montini at No. 23 Sandburg, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>This looks to be the first real test for Montini (1-0), which coasted past outmanned Hoopeston 48-0 last week for its 25th straight win. Five-star quarterback Israel Abrams, a Miami commit, threw for 192 yards and three touchdowns while playing just two quarters. Linebackers Ben Evenson and Orlando Greco each had two tackles for loss. Sandburg (1-0) was missing its returning starting quarterback, Sean Ruisz, in a 28-6 win against Riverside-Brookfield, but backup Max Fahey threw for 214 yards and four TDs.</p><h3>No. 6 Oswego at No. 12 Geneva, 7 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Junior running back Ammar Banire — who has offers from Illinois, Indiana and Iowa among others — piled up 286 all-purpose yards and five touchdowns behind a big, experienced offensive line as Oswego (1-0) beat Neuqua Valley 44-22 last week. Iowa State-bound defensive back Dontrell Young leads the Panthers defense. Geneva (1-0) has one of the state's elite pass-and-catch duos in quarterback Ben Peterson (Eastern Michigan) and receiver Bennett Konkey (Illinois), the defending Class 3A state champ in the 100 and 200 meters. Kinkey returned the opening kickoff for a touchdown and finished with 279 all-purpose yards in a 28-14 win against Libertyville last week.</p><h3>No. 15 St. Rita at No. 10 Glenbard West, 1:30 p.m. Saturday</h3><p>In his varsity starting debut, senior quarterback John Fennell of St. Rita (0-1) threw TD passes of 37 and 35 yards to TJ Burgos in a 28-21 loss to Providence. Glenbard West (1-0) has long been known for its deep and productive ground game. But this year the Hilltoppers feature an elite passing game led by quarterback AJ Rayford and tight end Brady Johnson, a Northwestern recruit who also is a game-changer on defense.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/23/high-school-football-schedule-ihsa-chicago-week-2-2026" >High school football schedule for Week 2 of the 2026 season</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/super-25-football-rankings/2026/08/23/high-school-football-rankings-chicago-illinois-sun-times-michael-obrien" >Michael O’Brien’s Super 25 high school football rankings for Week 2</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3>No. 17 York at No. 18 Nazareth, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Every week brings plenty of intriguing quarterback matchups. This one features York's Zack Assaad, who passed for two touchdowns and ran for another as the Dukes (1-0) got past Glenbrook South 20-17 last week. Purdue-bound lineman Owen Roberts leads an experienced York defense. In his debut for Nazareth — a 35-21 loss to IC Catholic — junior transfer JJ Chapman passed for 303 yards and one TD. The Roadrunners had some key players out with injury last week, but are one of the state's top Class 6A teams when at full strength.</p><h3>No. 22 Lyons at Wheaton-Warrenville South, 7:30 p.m. Friday</h3><p>Lyons (1-0) knocked off Barrington 24-19 last week, helping the West Suburban Silver seal a 7-0 opening week, as veteran running back EJ Kuhlman rushed for 132 yards. Linebackers Cole Harris and Aidan Webster helped to contain the Broncos' powerful ground game and the Lions won the turnover battle 2-0. Junior three-sport standout AJ Rogers threw for 201 yards and two touchdowns and Trent Simpson broke off a 75-yard touchdown run as Wheaton-Warrenville South (1-0) beat Naperville Central 27-7 last week.</p>

entries.title: Bears training-camp report No. 20: DT Gervon Dexter (hamstring) not with team in Tennessee
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Breaking down <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ Thursday training camp practice with the Titans:</p><p><b>What happened</b><br>The teams went about two and a half hours in the middle of the day with the temperature in the high 80s and high humidity. Several Bears players came to the sideline with apparent cramps.</p><p><b>Heated competition</b><br>The story of the day was a late-practice hit by Bears safety Xavier Woods on Titans wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson that knocked Robinson out of practice. Read more <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/27/titans-smolder-after-bears-s-xavier-woods-cheap-blindside-hit-on-wr-wandale-robinson-in-joint-practice" target="_blank" >here</a>.</p><p><b>Odeyingbo looks good</b><br>Bears defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo, coming off a season in which he had one sack in eight games before tearing his Achilles, had at least two would-be sacks on Titans quarterback Cam Ward. As usual, players weren’t allowed to hit the quarterbacks, and referees generally let plays continue unless it was painfully obvious.</p><p><b>Notable absence</b><br>Bears defensive tackle Gervon Dexter has been the subject of trade speculation lately and exited mid-practice Tuesday. Bears coach Ben Johnson said he has a hamstring injury and didn’t travel to Tennessee.</p><p><b>Halftime</b><br>The Bears and Titans took a break about halfway through their practice and players went into the air-conditioning bubble for several minutes. That’s relatively rare in the NFL, and the Bears haven’t done it in any recent camps. “It was good simulation for actual gametime because you’re going to come out hot and there’s going to be a halftime in the game and you’ve got to be able to maintain that,” defensive tackle Grady Jarrett said.</p><p><b>What’s next?</b><br>The Bears and Titans play a preseason game Saturday, and roster cuts for the regular season are due Sunday.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Good Good Golf loses PGA Tour event and Callaway sponsorships
entries.summary: <p>ATLANTA — Good Good Golf lost its partnership with Callaway on Thursday and no longer will be title sponsor of a PGA Tour event in November as the fallout continued over a video for a new Callaway driver that showed a man shoving a woman to the ground who was trying to touch the golf club.</p><p>Good Good, among the most popular in the YouTube Golf space, has said it was meant to be a spinoff from the movie, "Obsession." But the criticism was immediate and relentless, and the pressure began mounting by the day.</p><p>Golf Channel postponed a Good Good reality show because a sponsor, reported to be Golf Galaxy, wanted its brand scrubbed from the telecast. Dick's Sporting Goods removed the apparel from its stories. And then Callaway said it was ending the three-year sponsorship.</p><p>The PGA Tour confirmed Good Good would not be title sponsor of the new Nov. 12-15 tournament in Austin, Texas. Officials said it would seek a new title sponsor.</p>

entries.title: Jennifer Custer drops out of race for Chicago school board president
entries.summary: <p><i>This story was </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/27/jennifer-custer-drops-out-of-race-for-cps-board-president/" target="_blank" ><i>originally published by Chalkbeat</i></a><i>, which is partnering with Chicago Public Media to cover the upcoming Chicago School Board elections. Sign up for their newsletters at </i><a class="Link" href="https://ckbe.at/newsletters" target="_blank" ><i>ckbe.at/newsletters</i></a><i>.</i></p><p>Jennifer Custer, an incumbent school board member, is withdrawing from the race to be the first elected Chicago Board of Education president.</p><p>In a statement, she said she filed paperwork Thursday with the Chicago Board of Elections to withdraw. Custer was the only candidate in the race whose petition signatures were not challenged.</p><p>“I am exiting because it became abundantly clear that various special interests are prepared to spend millions of dollars in this race,” she wrote in the statement. “Going up against that kind of spending in our political system creates an uphill battle that I ultimately decided I did not want to put my family, endorsers, volunteers, and supporters through.”</p><p>Custer did not make an endorsement, but left the door open to doing so. Four other candidates remain: Jessica Biggs, a former CPS principal and incumbent school board member; Hilario Dominguez, political director for the Chicago Teachers Union and former special education teacher; Victor Henderson, an attorney, and Sendhil Revuluri, a consultant and former vice president of the school board appointed by then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot.</p><p>“I know the other candidates in this race well, and I will ask the same question I have asked throughout my time on the Board: Who shares my North Star of doing what is best for our children?” Custer wrote.</p><p>The former suburban educator and mom of three <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2024/11/05/school-board-election-results-2024/" target="_blank" ><u>narrowly won her seat in 2024</u></a> over Michelle Pierre, who is now running again to represent district 1b. Custer <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2024/09/25/school-board-elections-2024-district-1-candidates-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u>had the support of the Chicago Teachers Union</u></a>, but forged a more independent path over the past two years serving on the board.</p><p>Recently, she was the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/13/chicago-public-schools-board-backs-revenue-referendums/" target="_blank" ><u>only no vote</u></a> on the board’s decision to put two non-binding referendums about raising new revenue for CPS on the November ballot. Both questions were put forward by Mayor Brandon Johnson’s allies and Custer was the only one of a more independent bloc of school board members to attend the meeting. She was also the <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/03/30/chicago-board-of-education-hires-macquline-king/" target="_blank" ><u>lone no vote</u></a> against hiring Chicago Public Schools CEO Macquline King as the permanent leader.</p><p>In July, Custer joined with six other school board members to vote <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsboe.org/content/documents/july_2026_vote_tally_update_v1.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>against an amended budget</u></a> that assumes $150 million more in state revenue. She also <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/03/22/cps-school-board-members-oppose-pension-payment/" target="_blank" ><u>voted against taking out a high-interest loan</u></a> last year to reimburse the city for a portion of a payment to a municipal pension fund that supports non-teaching staff and retirees in CPS.</p><p>Custer’s fundraising lagged behind the other candidates in the race. One of her top donors has been the political action committee of the Operating Engineers Local 150, where her husband, Jeremy, is the political director. In April, she <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/04/17/chicago-public-schools-board-races-draw-cash/" target="_blank" ><u>told Chalkbeat one of her biggest campaign expenses has been child care</u></a>, which is a permissible expenditure under state campaign finance laws. Arranging care for her children had allowed her to visit schools, meet with potential supporters, and attend board meetings, she said.</p><p>In her statement, Custer thanked her campaign staff and her family; "especially my three little ones, who have seen less of me than they deserve,” she wrote.</p><p>Prior to serving on Chicago’s school board, Custer worked as a paraprofessional, and classroom teacher and administrator in school districts in Wisconsin and Chicago’s suburbs. She served for two years as president of the teachers union in Itasca and was an assistant principal and interim principal in Addison School District 4.</p><p><i>Becky Vevea is the bureau chief for Chalkbeat Chicago. Contact Becky at </i><a class="Link" href="mailto:bvevea@chalkbeat.org" target="_blank" ><i><u>bvevea@chalkbeat.org</u></i></a><i>.   </i></p><p><i>Chalkbeat is a nonprofit news organization </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/08/27/jennifer-custer-drops-out-of-race-for-cps-board-president/" target="_blank" ><i>covering public education</i></a><i>.</i></p>

entries.title: Heather Mack's ex-boyfriend will stay in jail while awaiting trial in Bali murder plot
entries.summary: <p>The ex-boyfriend of Heather Mack<b> </b>who’s long been accused of beating her<b> </b>mother<b> </b>to death<b> </b>in a brazen international murder plot will remain in federal custody while he awaits trial early next year.</p><p>Tommy<b> </b>Schaefer, 33,<b> </b>asked<b> </b>this month<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/14/heather-mack-tommy-shaefer-murder" target="_blank" >to be let out of jail</a> and put on home confinement to deal with his ongoing health issues. U.S. District Judge Matthew<b> </b>Kennelly<b> </b>denied his request<b> </b>at the end of a<b> </b>half-hour hearing<b> </b>Thursday<b> </b>at the Dirksen Federal Courthouse.</p><p>The judge also agreed to push back Schaefer’s trial until March 15,<b> </b>but insisted he’ll allow no more delays. Mack and Schaefer are accused of plotting<b> </b>the<b> </b>2014<b> </b>murder<b> </b>of Mack’s mother, Sheila<b> </b>von<b> </b>Wiese-Mack, in Indonesia to access her $1.5 million estate.</p><p>“[Schaefer] crossed the world to brutally kill another human being because he hoped it would bring him financial rewards,” prosecutors wrote in a court filing<b> </b>this week.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/17/24039349/heather-mack-gets-26-years-in-federal-prison-for-the-murder-of-her-mother-in-bali" >Heather Mack gets 26 years for murder of mom in Bali after stark testimony from family</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The killing triggered tabloid headlines around the world<b> </b>after von Wiese-Mack’s body was found stuffed in a suitcase outside the posh St. Regis Bali Resort. Mack and Schaefer then spent several years<b> </b>incarcerated in Indonesia<b> </b>for von Wiese-Mack’s murder.</p><p>However, they were also charged in the United States with conspiracy<b> </b>and<b> </b>obstruction of justice. Mack <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/11/3/22761085/heather-mack-returns-chicago-ohare-fbi-charged-conspiracy" target="_blank" >returned to the United States</a> in 2021<b> </b>and was sentenced<b> </b>by Kennelly to<b> </b>26 years in prison. Schaefer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/heather-mack/2026/02/25/chicago-crime-heather-mack-tommy-schaefer-fbi-bali-indonesia" target="_blank" >returned<b> </b>in February</a>, and he’s been held in federal custody since.</p><p>Schaefer lawyer Michael<b> </b>Baker<b> </b>argued Thursday<b> </b>his client<b> </b>doesn’t have the financial means to flee. But Kennelly said the same might have been said of Schaefer<b> </b>before von Wiese-Mack’s murder, which occurred when Schaefer was 21.</p><p>“And yet, here we are,” Kennelly said.</p><div </b>COVID-19<b> </b>in Indonesia<b> </b>and has since been diagnosed with<b> </b>a post-infectious condition. Cardiac evaluations were pending<b> </b>as of Aug. 14.</p><p>Baker asked Kennelly to place Schaefer on home incarceration<b> </b>with a third-party custodian.</p><p>“This is a 12-year-old alleged offense,” Baker told the judge Thursday. “It’s arising out of a relationship that no longer exists with Ms. Mack, and a scheme that no longer exists with Ms. Mack. There’s no identifiable person that Mr. Schaefer poses a risk to in this community.”</p><p>Kennelly wasn’t convinced.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2021/11/3/22761085/heather-mack-returns-chicago-ohare-fbi-charged-conspiracy" >Heather Mack, Tommy Schaefer charged in U.S. indictment with conspiring to kill Mack’s mother</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Mack broached the idea of killing her mother with Schaefer as early as February 2014, the feds say. Schaefer wrote in a Facebook chat that month, “that b---- heather is crazy”<b> </b>and added, “she asked me to find someone to kill her mom for 50k.”</p><p>Mack ultimately enlisted Schaefer, secretly booking a $12,000 plane ticket for him so he could rendezvous with her while she vacationed with her mother in Bali in August 2014, according to prosecutors.</p><p>Then, over the course of nearly 40 minutes on the morning of Aug. 12, 2014, prosecutors say Mack and Schaefer exchanged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/9/24/18424089/heather-mack-traded-giddy-tense-texts-with-boyfriend-before-mom-s-murder" target="_blank" >tense, excited text messages</a> as they prepared to murder von Wiese-Mack. They allegedly used the phrase “saying hi”<b> </b>as code for the killing, and they referred to each other as Bonnie and Clyde.</p><p>Soon after, prosecutors say, von Wiese-Mack “was brutally beaten after being taken by surprise as she lay in her hotel bed.”</p><p>Mack’s<b> </b>plea agreement<b> </b>alleged<b> </b>Schaefer<b> </b>“repeatedly beat [von Wiese-Mack] in the head and face”<b> </b>using the metal handle<b> </b>of a fruit bowl<b> </b>before<b> </b>she<b> </b>died.</p>

entries.title: Titans smolder after Bears S Xavier Woods' 'cheap' blindside hit on WR Wan'Dale Robinson in joint practice
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — The Titans were steaming Thursday after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> safety Xavier Woods delivered a blindside hit to wide receiver Wan’Dale Robinson that knocked him out of practice. The play immediately was flagged for a personal foul, and the drill devolved into a sprawling scuffle between the teams.</p><p>Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll rushed toward the scrum immediately and yelled, “That’s [expletive] [garbage],” at Woods, who continued yelling at opposing players from the sideline afterward.</p><p>Titans coach Robert Saleh’s only reaction to it was, “Cheap,” and he said Robinson was being evaluated for a possible concussion. Left guard Peter Skoronski said, “That’s teach tape 101 of what not to do.”</p><p>Woods, though, has quickly endeared himself to the Bears with that style of play. He signed about three weeks ago and immediately jumped into competition for a starting job.</p><p>“We practice a certain way, the way we want to play ball,” defensive tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/03/13/bears-gm-ryan-poles-boldly-bets-on-joe-thuney-grady-jarrett" >Grady Jarrett</a> said. “Nothing is done with malice, but we’ve got to play our style of defense the way we want to at all times. Sometimes things happen.”</p><p>Woods was not available to reporters after practice.</p>

entries.title: Losing trip out West can’t ding Cubs’ confidence in championship chase: ‘Everybody knows what the mission is’
entries.summary: <p>Pete Crow-Armstrong’s equipment is never safe, not even in the best of times.</p><p>But this road trip out West was not among the best of times, and the Diamondbacks’ game broadcast Wednesday was able to stitch together a somewhat lengthy montage of Crow-Armstrong taking out his frustrations over a 1-for-12 series in Arizona on helmets, gloves, bats and other gear.</p><p>If you run a Dick’s Sporting Goods and see this guy coming, maybe close up early.</p><p>These stretches will happen in even the greatest of individual seasons, and Crow-Armstrong is having one of those, doing the unthinkable by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/05/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-shohei-ohtani-nl-mvp-race-dodgers-playoffs-craig-counsell-shota-imanaga" >challenging two-way star Shohei Ohtani</a> for the National League MVP.</p><p>But a tough road trip at the plate for Crow-Armstrong — it was only so tough; prior to three quiet days in the desert, he had four hits, two of them homers, in three days in Seattle — coincided with a somewhat chaotic stretch for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>, who were walked off three times in six days out West, flying back to Chicago having dropped four of six contests.</p><p>“You don’t let a couple disappointing days fluster you,” left fielder Ian Happ said Tuesday. “You just come right back. That’s kind of been the M.O. of this team, you move on and tackle the next day.”</p><p>Widen the lens a tad, and the Cubs were involved in five walk-off games in nine days, having won the first two games of last week’s series with the White Sox in walk-off fashion.</p><p>“A little extreme,” manager Craig Counsell said Wednesday. “But you’re on the other side of it, too. … Major League Baseball teaches you really fast that you’ve got to think about the game for a little bit and then you cut the cord with that and move onto the next day.”</p><p>Righty reliever Jacob Webb <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-walk-off-loss-diamondbacks-clay-holmes-kevin-gausman-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-bullpen" >served up a pair of walk-off homers</a> in as many outings, but don’t fear a closer crisis; he’s the same pitcher who recorded 24 consecutive scoreless outings coming into the trip.</p><p>Perhaps more concerning, from a pitching standpoint, is lefty Shota Imanaga getting yanked after recording only six outs against the Mariners, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/23/cubs-mariners-brewers-nl-central-standings-shota-imanaga-stats-starting-rotation-playoffs" >the shortest outing of his career</a>. Fellow southpaw Matthew Boyd had another bumpy ride in Seattle, but he bounced back nicely Wednesday in Phoenix, delivering his finest outing of the month.</p><p>The newcomers in the rotation <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/25/cubs-kevin-gausman-starting-pitching-world-series-playoffs-postseason-michael-conforto-ian-happ-pete-crow-armstrong" >looked dominant against the in-the-hunt D-backs</a>, with righties Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes combining to throw 14 shutout innings and allow only five singles.</p><p>And while Crow-Armstrong was busy chucking anything he could find all over Chase Field — and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/26/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-balk-umpires-diamondbacks-eduardo-rodriguez-craig-counsell-matthew-boyd" >going off on umpires after they missed a balk</a> Wednesday — this was the same trip on which the Cubs’ lineup set a new franchise mark with 30 consecutive runs scored against opponents over the course of three days.</p><p>In other words, this trip didn’t ding this team’s confidence, even if it’s lost three of its last four series.</p><p>“Road trips are tough in August, and the whole month of August is a grind,” Crow-Armstrong said Wednesday. “We’re all just trying to keep our heads above water. There was a lot of good on this road trip.”</p><p>The Cubs still woke up Thursday with the fifth best record in baseball and their sights on chasing the same World Series goals they’ve had since the beginning.</p><p>“One of the impressive things about this group is it doesn’t change,” Happ said. “There’s been that identity — or ‘hunger,’ if you want to call it that — since Day 1. We came into spring training with it.</p><p>“The desire to go out and play this exceptional brand of baseball, it’s what the group brings every day. It’s the fun part of playing with a veteran group that’s been doing this so long. Everybody knows what the mission is, and it’s the guiding light.”</p><p>Whether it’s a veteran of last year’s champs seeing “something special” or the fresh eyes of a guy who pitched in the World Series last fall, these Cubs — even far from the best of times — still know where they’re capable of going.</p><p>“The sky’s the limit,” Gausman said Monday. “This defense, this offense, the pitchers that we have here, it’s a really great team. There’s not many weaknesses.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable rates, celebrates — and self-evaluates — as upstart team hits home stretch
entries.summary: <p>One year ago, when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> had exactly 29 games to go — same as now — a bumbling columnist poked around the clubhouse and dugout asking questions based on a rather flimsy premise.</p><p>Look, you try coming up with dazzling late-summer storylines on a team bound for its third straight 100-plus-loss finish.</p><p>The premise that day: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/09/01/white-sox-2025-loss-cause-if-100-is-inevitable-at-least-try-to-stay-under-106" target="_blank" >How important was it to the Sox to avoid the ignominy of triple-digit “Ls”</a>? They’d have to finish with a 15-14 “tear” to do it. (They went 12-17 instead to end up 60-102.)</p><p>Then-rookie manager Will Venable humored me on the subject despite its superficiality. There are no parades for 99-loss teams, after all.</p><p>“Of course, no one wants to lose 100 games,” he said, “but I don’t think it will come up as a topic of conversation with us.”</p><p>The good news: There are far better things to discuss when a team is 70-63 and in first place heading into the final 29 of the regular season.</p><p>The Sox have pitching issues, yet they hit the road for Minnesota having won eight of their last 13 and 11 of 18. They were a bit gassed by the end of 16 straight games without a day off, yet they more than survived the gauntlet. Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery are slumping badly, but red-hot Tristan Peters and Miguel Vargas are carrying the lineup just fine.</p><p>Have the Sox — in first place since July 4 — reached the point where even when they stink, they don’t stink? It seems so.</p><p>Players claim they saw all this coming a year ago.</p><p>“I’m not surprised where we’re at,” said second baseman Chase Meidroth, who added five hits to the mix as the Sox beat the Rangers in the last two games of a 4-3 homestand.</p><p>“Yeah, for sure I thought we’d be here,” said third baseman Vargas, owner of a 1.022 OPS in August. “This is our identity now.”</p><p>But Venable? He was a bit more thoughtful when I asked him how much he would have believed a year ago — on a scale of 1 to 10 — the Sox would be where they are now.</p><p>“A 5,” he said after some consideration. “I don’t want to say I didn’t expect us to be here, but I also don’t want to say I [did].”</p><p>Normally, Venable — like his boss, general manager Chris Getz — holds even tighter than most to the “one game at a time” mantra that reveals little of good use, narratively speaking. As we talked Wednesday before the Sox walloped the Rangers 10-4, he loosened his grip on the wheel a little.</p><p>“Obviously, we know it’s about tonight’s game,” he said. “But I think that it’s totally fine to take a step back and — I don’t want to say celebrate — but, I don’t know, you know what? Maybe that is the right word. It’s OK to take a step back and celebrate the fact that we’ve made a ton of progress. And there are indicators everywhere; certainly in our record, and you just look out on the field and we have really good players that play the game the right way. We have a ton of great things happening behind the scenes. …</p><p>“[We’re] in a much better spot than we were a year ago.”</p><p>I asked him to do some self-evaluation as a second-year manager. He has a good shot to win the American League manager of the year award, but to some extent that’s superficial, too. At 43, is he good at this?</p><p>“A lot better than last year,” he said.</p><p>Venable hasn’t been perfect. For one thing, there was the blunder during a game this month when he made a second visit to the mound during the first inning, forcing starting pitcher Noah Schultz to depart prematurely with the bullpen already thin on available arms. That one stung.</p><p>“But it’s OK to make mistakes. We make mistakes and we get better,” he said. “I’ve been part of that and want to be a leader with that mindset. I feel like I’ve grown a ton, but I have a long way to go, too.</p><p>“If I’m evaluating myself, am I creating an environment for our players to be at their best? I think there’s a lot of good things to point to in that area; there’s things I’m learning every day that I can do for our group, our environment. There’s also the in-game stuff; I have a ton of support with that and it’s something we’re all working at.”</p><p>These Sox are on target to become baseball’s most unexpected division winner, whereupon — just being honest — next to no one outside Sox walls will pick them to beat anybody in the playoffs.</p><p>Next year, though, there’s a decent chance the Sox will go in as the favorites to win the AL Central. With the right offseason maneuvering by Getz and his crew, the Sox should move closer to what they view as contention for something even bigger. Eventually, a decision will have to be made about whether or not Venable is the skipper to steer the Sox over the top.</p><p>At this point, there’s no reason to think Getz has any doubts about the guy he already has. Let’s be clear on that.</p><p>Yeah, yeah: Flimsy premise alert.</p><p>But there is a history in the sport — and in Chicago, notably, of recent vintage — of teams bailing on first-time managers just as so-called winning windows open wide. A month after Cubs chairman Tom Ricketts called David Ross “our guy,” Ross was kicked to the curb and replaced by star Craig Counsell. If Counsell hadn’t been there for the stealing, Ross surely would’ve gotten another season.</p><p>Before that, the Cubs dumped Rick Renteria after one season to go after Joe Maddon. Renteria, poor guy, later was gut-punched by the Sox, freeing chairman Jerry Reinsdorf to make a buddy movie with Tony La Russa.</p><p>Venable humored me on this one, too.</p><p>“I’ll say this, these jobs have such volatility that you don’t make any assumptions about what the future looks like, whether that’s a positive thing or a negative thing,” he said. “Truthfully, you just are grateful for every day and you know the reality of the industry is that everyone is replaceable and eventually, at some point, you’re not asked back.</p><p>“I think that has nothing necessarily to do with my situation, but it is reality.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/01/white-sox-chris-getz-chicago-saw-success-coming-even-if-others-including-me-didnt" target="_blank" >White Sox GM Chris Getz saw success coming, even if others — including me — didn’t</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/09/01/white-sox-2025-loss-cause-if-100-is-inevitable-at-least-try-to-stay-under-106" target="_blank" >White Sox’ 2025 loss cause: If 100 is inevitable, at least try to stay under 106</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: All Seasons Orchard in Woodstock to unveil Dolly Parton corn maze
entries.summary: <p>All Seasons Orchard heard Dolly Parton when she said “if you don't like the road you’re walking, start paving another one.”</p><p>The popular seasonal attraction in suburban Woodstock has paved a new course through its crops and on Saturday will unveil its larger-than-life homage to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/25/dolly-parton-music-star-actor-and-beloved-figure-who-spanned-generations-has-died-at-80" target="_blank" >country superstar who passed away Tuesday</a> at the age of 80. It’s a 6-acre corn maze carved in Parton’s likeness, with her wide smile and big bouffant part of the course, along with the inscription, “An American Treasure.”</p><p>“We hope it’s a good opportunity for people who love Dolly to come out and remember her and the joy that she brought to life,” said All Seasons marketing director Kamille Combs.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div In recent years, the property has partnered with Utah “agri-tainment” developer The MAiZE on a nationwide Country Music Corn Maze campaign, where previous designs have honored Reba McEntire, Luke Bryan and Lainey Wilson most recently in 2025. (With the 2026 launch, The MAiZE also tagged onto the America 250 celebrations adding the “American Treasure” line.)</p><p>The Dolly Parton concept had been in the works for nearly three years, going through the approval process with Parton and her Imagination Library book-gifting program. </p><p>All Seasons Orchard had just unveiled the 2026 Dolly design on Monday, just a day before Parton passed away and the announcement featured a <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/v/1BpoBnLUgi/" target="_blank" ><u>video</u></a> from Parton herself. “Grab your friends, gather up the family and come on out to one of my favorite farms for a little fun, laughter and a real good reason to get lost,” the star said in the message.</p><p>Proceeds from this season’s ticket sales will be donated to local Imagination Library chapters, continuing the mission to provide free books for children. All Seasons Orchard — one of 20 farms across the country and the only farm in Illinois with the Dolly maze — will also make a direct donation to the organization, says Combs. “In light of the statement that's been put out by her family … inviting people to donate to the library, we want to support that. We will be discussing other ways we can help, too and brainstorming additional options that we can give people an opportunity to remember Dolly, her legacy and her memories.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-630000" name="image-630000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a910964/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F03%2F3b%2F24174cb64ee99c5af469c778a126%2Fdollymaze-260829-10.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/93cd7ca/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F03%2F3b%2F24174cb64ee99c5af469c778a126%2Fdollymaze-260829-10.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d2ba27/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F03%2F3b%2F24174cb64ee99c5af469c778a126%2Fdollymaze-260829-10.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Annette Jenkins (left) and Dan Weckerly stand in front of the entrance to the Dolly Parton corn maze at All Seasons Orchard at 14510 IL-Rte 176 in Woodstock, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d2ba27/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F03%2F3b%2F24174cb64ee99c5af469c778a126%2Fdollymaze-260829-10.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ce5de95/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F03%2F3b%2F24174cb64ee99c5af469c778a126%2Fdollymaze-260829-10.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8d2ba27/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6122x3436+0+324/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F03%2F3b%2F24174cb64ee99c5af469c778a126%2Fdollymaze-260829-10.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Annette Jenkins (left) and Dan Weckerly stand in front of the entrance to the Dolly Parton corn maze at All Seasons Orchard.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In addition to the maze, which took a half-day to cut into the field and will take patrons roughly 30-60 minutes to complete, there will also be a “life-size” photo op, says Combs, and an interactive game throughout the maze where guests can test their Parton trivia.</p><p>“There are 10 different prompts where, if you answer a question correctly about Dolly and the Imagination Library, you’ll get a clue about the right way to go. And wrong answers will send you in the wrong direction,” Combs said. “It’s a great opportunity for people to learn about her and see how much they know.”</p><p>For All Seasons, the maze is a way to tie back into Parton’s farming roots. “We love <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DceNXgPJyZ9/?hl=en" target="_blank" ><u>the quote</u></a> the family put out this week about how ‘Dolly was a farmer just like her daddy. He farmed the soil and she farmed songs and happiness.’ We too are a family-run orchard, and I think it's part of the reason we wanted to feature her in our maze,” Combs said. “We know her roots, we know her love and passion for farming and agriculture. And we know her life was about trying to bring joy and happiness to people. So hopefully we're continuing and honoring that as well.”</p><p><i>For information on hours and ticket pricing for the Dolly Parton corn maze, go to </i><a class="Link" href="http://allseasonsorchard.com" target="_blank" ><i><u>allseasonsorchard.com</u></i></a><i>.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-160000" name="module-160000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Celebrate Dolly Parton at these Chicago-area events</h3><br><b>Aug. 27: </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1GVmCmFJvr/" target="_blank" ><u>Nicky’s of Beverly</u></a>, 10500 S. Western Ave., will be spinning Parton’s records courtesy of DJ John from Beverly Records.<br><br><b>Aug. 28: </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.hideoutchicago.com/shows/the-hideout-celebrates-dolly-parton-28-aug" target="_blank" ><u>Hideout Inn</u></a>, 1354 W Wabansia Ave., will be spinning Parton’s famous tunes and screen a double feature of “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas” and “9 to 5.”<br><br><b>Aug. 29:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DcfCZckqyK4/" target="_blank" ><u>Roscoe’s Tavern</u></a>, 3356 N. Halsted St., will offer a special edition of its SERVED! Drag Brunch, the “Queen of Country Edition” paying tribute to Dolly.<br><br><b>Aug. 30: </b><a class="Link" href="https://www.sidetrackchicago.com/calendar/" target="_blank" ><u>Sidetrack</u></a>, 3349 N. entries.title: Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' in the U.S.
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday he is <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-renaming-lake-ontario-65bbd47925365ffd5d9522cf4b2e4bc8" target="_blank" >renaming Lake Ontario</a> to be known as “Lake America” in the United States as he exacerbates his trade war with Canada.</p><p>The Republican president signed an <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/08/honoring-the-american-history-of-the-great-lakes-and-renaming-lake-ontario-as-lake-america/" target="_blank" >executive order</a> directing the Interior Department to update the lake's name in the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow his preferred naming convention, however.</p><p>Trump has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/canada-us-trade-tariffs-trump-857ef76b20a766e370d70176135b678e" target="_blank" >50% tariffs</a> on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. Trump has been needling America’s northern neighbor since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the U.S. once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/how-canada-could-become-us-state-42360e10ded96c0046fd11eaaf55ab88" target="_blank" >51st state</a>.</p><p>Canada responded to Trump’s import taxes this week by imposing retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.</p><p>Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read “Lake America.”</p><p>On the other wide of the president was another map with the words, “MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER.”</p><p>The lake is one of multiple Great Lakes that the U.S. and Canada share borders along.</p><p>The office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>There is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water and Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.</p><p>Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded insults with Trump, this week brushed aside the prospect of Trump changing the lake's name as “a lot of rhetoric."</p><p>The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people’s word “oniatarí:io,” that means “lake of shining waters.” The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div geopolitical message, “Canada’s been ripping us off for a long time” on trade and military issues.</p><p>“They wanted to be treated like a state and they’re not a state,” the president said. “We just can’t do that anymore.”</p><p>“We love the people of Canada,” Trump added. “I don’t think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they’ll change. I really don’t know. It doesn’t make much difference.”</p><p>The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America."</p><p>Trump scribbled his name with a Sharpie pen on the executive order then held it up for the cameras, offering, “And we filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else.”</p><p>“We’ve notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So, we’ve done everything that you have to do,” he said. “And this is official, effective immediately.”</p><p>The executive order Trump signed shows that the changes in fact are supposed to be made within 30 days.</p><p>He also suggested his push to rename bodies of water may not be finished.</p><p>“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean,” Trump said. “So maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them.”</p><p><i>Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto contributed to this report.</i></p>

entries.title: Newly drafted White Sox prospect Alex Weingartner offers impressive physical toolkit
entries.summary: <p>Of the four prep players the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> extended seven-figure bonuses to last month, in the most expensive draft class in MLB history, outfielder Alex Weingartner is easily the fastest.</p><p>The 18-year-old New Jersey two-way star ran the 60-yard dash in a blazing 6.24 seconds at the Super 60 showcase in suburban McCook this January with Sox staffers in attendance, before he touched 94 mph off the mound later the same afternoon.</p><p>Along with the ability to blister a home run earlier this week in “bridge league” action that rocketed off a field at Camelback Ranch in Arizona at 107 mph exit velocity, Weingartner has a physical toolkit that inspired the White Sox to pick him in the sixth round, but for a $1.4 million signing bonus that constitutes late second-round value.</p><p>Just don’t call it “raw” athleticism. It’s the product of work.</p><p>“I definitely wasn't always fast, I was like a baby deer; my limbs, everything was all over the place,” Weingartner told the Sun-Times. “My older brother, he was always really fast, and my goal was to try and beat him. That helped me in the long run, just being by his side and training with him.”</p><p>For a teenager, Weingartner is impressively filled out, with enough strength to swing hard without the moving parts and big loading actions typical of younger hitters. The combination of centerfield-grade speed, a plus throwing arm and eventually above-average raw power inspired the Sox to pick a direction for a prospect who has shown a little bit of everything.</p><p>“I was just doing both until somebody told me in a way like what route I was going to do,” Weingartner said of abandoning his two-way player status. “I definitely started loving hitting more and really being an athlete and loving that. That drove that decision, and then just the White Sox saw me as a talented outfielder, and they made the decision easy for me.”</p><p>Pitching prospects have an incredibly high fail rate of their own, but the risk the White Sox are incurring is a hit tool that gives league scouts pause about Weingartner’s ability to make enough contact to actualize his impressive physicality. Sox hitting development has long-term plans to add more rhythm and movement to Weingartner’s setup over time. But the player himself is already raving about the improvements in contact ability he’s seen from being exposed to high velocity and spin from the pitching machines at the White Sox complex.</p><p>“If you've never seen it before and you've never been exposed to it, it's difficult to evaluate whether or not somebody will be successful,” Weingartner contends. “Showing up here and [Sox coaches] helping me constantly, every day, I show up to the field to be a better hitter and understand my swing more. It's progressed very rapidly.”</p><p>Is Weingartner a future White Sox mainstay? Or is he a future occupier of the sort of “middle class” of prospect that general manager Chris Getz said the farm system lacked to deal from at this month’s trade deadline? In either case, Weingartner feels he’s already on the way.</p><p>“I’m nowhere near my angle of where I want to be with my swing and what I need to be at the plate,” Weingartner said. “But I think that hit tool, at least for me and in the back of my mind, the question of whether or not I was going to be successful at this level, went away.”</p><h3><b>Roster moves</b></h3><p>The White Sox optioned Jonathan Cannon on Thursday’s off day, recalling reliever Tyler Davis from Triple-A to take his place. The move essentially adds a fresh arm to a bullpen taxed by 16 games in as many days, to where <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/26/jonathan-cannon-white-sox-pitching-staff-touting-an-overhauled-arsenal-jake-burger-tristan-peters-franchise-record-davis-martin-kyle-teel" target="_blank" ><u>Cannon covering the last three innings of Wednesday’s 10-4 victory</u></a> over the Rangers was sorely needed.</p><p>Davis, an undrafted rookie signed away from the independent league Oakland Ballers in 2024 for his overpowering mid-90s four-seam fastball, has posted a 4.10 ERA in his major league action this year, and even recorded his first career save in May. His demotion to Triple-A was driven by control problems, and even though Davis has a 5.40 ERA with Charlotte during August, a 13-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio this month is encouraging.</p><p>Outfielder Rikuu Nishida was also optioned after being recalled on Tuesday to fill a roster spot vacated by veteran Andrew Benintendi, who was placed on bereavement leave. Nishida did not appear in a game during his second stint of the year in Chicago, as the Sox opted to start <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/25/white-sox-trade-deadline-acquisitions-huascar-brazoban-injured-list-brenton-doyle-luis-castillo-jose-urquidy-joey-bart-jake-rogers-andrew-benintendi-chris-getz-walker-mckinven" target="_blank" ><u>the recently acquired Brenton Doyle</u></a> in center, who compiled back-to-back multi-hit games and clocked a three-run homer in Wednesday’s victory.</p><p>By Friday, Benintendi will have spent the minimum three days on the bereavement list, and will be eligible to be activated ahead of the team’s series against the Twins in Minneapolis.</p><p></p><div class="PageListL" entries.title: How are kids supposed to learn anything if AI does their work for them?
entries.summary: <p><i>"The technologies are now able to credibly complete most undergraduate assignments."</i><br><i>— Washington Post</i></p><p>I bumbled into the job. A colleague knew I had interviewed celebrities for a magazine, and asked if I could talk to his journalism class at Loyola about the challenges of writing profiles of the famous. So I leaned on the podium for an hour and prattled about walking a golf course in Jamaica with Arnold Palmer and talking jazz over dinner with trumpet legend Dizzy Gillespie.</p><p>"You're better than this than I am," my colleague said, afterward, suggesting I teach. So I ambled over to the dean's office and he and gave me a class teaching feature writing.</p><p>I started the students off with writing profiles, the most basic story. You've got your material — someone's life — already assembled. You've got the narrative arc — their career path — waiting to guide you. I signed up 20 real Chicago personalities — TV journalist Carol Marin, firebrand Rev. Michael Pfleger, Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas — put their names on index cards, and handed them out to the class.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-040000" name="module-040000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Opinion bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Opinion</h2></div> </div><p>We moved slowly. First the kids developed questions for their subjects, based on their life stories. I reviewed those. Then the interviews. Eventually, I had 20 finished profiles before me.</p><p>Nineteen students understood the assignment. But reading one, on entrepreneur Leslie Hindman, suddenly the tone of the writing shifted dramatically. The profile was describing her business, a Chicago auction house, and it was like moving from gravel to asphalt.</p><p><i>"This is boilerplate,"</i> I thought. <i>"She took this off the internet."</i> I plugged a paragraph into a search engine. Up it popped, on the auction house site. Word for word. It took 30 seconds to find.</p><p>On the first day of class, I had made a little speech: "I know you can steal stuff from online. Don't do it. Because I'll find out and you'll fail." <br>I didn't want to confront the student alone, so dragged the dean in with me, as backup. I expected the student to be in trouble, maybe expelled. </p><p>That didn't happen. He explained to me that the dire consequences for plagiarism that Loyola warns about were more notional than real. The customer is always right. So together we gently tried to explain to the student who swiped copy why what she did was wrong. It was a struggle.</p><p>I thought the student might be ashamed, at least apologetic. She wasn't. She was defiant. This was research! She was a single mother! She needed this class credit! She needed this degree!</p><p>I pointed out that, yeah, you need the degree because it means something. If the only thing a Loyola degree represents is that you can deftly swipe other people's work, then it doesn't mean much, does it?</p><p>The solution I generously offered — redo the profile without plagiarizing this time — was batted away as draconian. She dropped the course, and huffed off in search of a less rigorous instructor. </p><p>Turns out, my student was years ahead of the curve. Now the great engines of technology align to help everyone farm out the creative process. Only suckers do the work.</p><p>Having artificial intelligence do your job for you, for all of us, might indeed be the future — I have no idea. As the guy who once wrote that cell phones were a fad, I shouldn't make predictions. Maybe we won't need to write, or read, anymore. AI will do both. We will be liberated to spend our days scrolling mindlessly through an endless stream of little AI-generated videos showing morbidly obese porch pirates getting their faces blasted with blue dye.</p><p>I like to think not, and am reminded of those years in the 1960s when the powers that be decided we would all take our nutrition in pill form. We were offered Space Food Sticks — gooey faux Tootsie Rolls with stellar aspirations — and Tang, the orange-colored liquid the astronauts supposedly drank.</p><p>Then a funny thing happened. Turns out, people didn't want to consume their food in a pill. They wanted to bake rough artisanal breads, and grow heritage apples, and make radicchio salads from greens grown in their own gardens. Chefs became celebrities.</p><p>Maybe we will feel that way about work someday. I already do. Looking back on my career, I didn't get famous and I didn't get rich. But I did do the work, myself. That is success. If a drone could have watched a heart transplant, or covered a church fire, or climbed halfway up the west communications mast of the Hancock Building, accompanying workers doing repairs, and AI could have written the resulting stories, I like to think I would have still done it, and done it better. These kids today don't know what they're missing. Someone ought to teach them.</p>

entries.title: What to know about Flock’s controversial license plate readers
entries.summary: <p>License plate readers have sparked a heated, nationwide debate over mass surveillance tools in law enforcement.</p><p>And Flock Safety, one of the more commonly known private security companies that markets plate readers, has found itself at the center.</p><p>Law enforcement officials insist Flock's plate-reader cameras are helpful crime-fighting tools, despite revelations that data from those cameras has been accessed by federal immigration agents and officials tracking abortions. Meanwhile, some cops have been accused of using the technology to stalk people, and activists have been charged with stealing Flock cameras. </p><p>Here’s what you need to know.</p><h3><b>What’s a license plate reader?</b></h3><p>License plate readers are cameras that turn photos of passing cars into text descriptions that can be searched in a database, using the make, model, license plate and location of a vehicle. Users can then set alerts and get notifications for specific vehicles and plates.</p><p>Plate readers are different than red light cameras and speed cameras, which are only triggered by alleged violations. The data from those traffic cameras typically isn’t shared outside the city that owns them.</p><h3><b>What’s Flock Safety? </b></h3><p>Flock is an Atlanta-based company that makes surveillance tools, including drones and gunshot-detection systems similar to ShotSpotter, the technology Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/02/13/mayor-johnson-to-end-shotspotter-deal-after-summer" target="_blank" >Mayor Brandon Johnson got rid of.</a></p><p>Flock’s license plate readers are used by more than 7,000 law enforcement agencies nationwide, including more than 500 in Illinois. They’re also used by colleges, such as the University of Illinois Chicago.</p><h3><b>Why is Flock controversial? </b></h3><p>There are questions about whether arrests stemming from Flock alerts are constitutional because plate-reader databases can be searched without a warrant in Illinois.</p><p>An audit by the Illinois secretary of state’s office found that Flock license plate data originating in Illinois had been accessed by out-of-state law enforcement officials <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/abortion/2025/06/12/license-plate-readers-illinois-abortion-immigration" target="_blank" >monitoring abortions</a> and immigration enforcement agents whose coordination with local police is limited.</p><p>Dozens of police officials across the country have also been accused of making unauthorized Flock searches — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" target="_blank" ><u>including some locally</u></a> — and many face criminal charges.</p><h3><b>How have people pushed back?</b></h3><p>Grassroots organizing movements have cropped up in some suburbs, including Woodstock and Warrenville, where residents have urged local officials to end agreements with Flock. Some municipalities, such as Evanston and Oak Park, have moved to end their contracts with Flock.</p><p>Amid the acrimonious nationwide fight over Flock, some activists in the suburbs have been accused of defacing and stealing Flock cameras and sensors. That includes three men <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/28/flock-license-plate-reader-lisle-bob-berlin" target="_blank" >charged with theft and criminal damage</a> to government property for allegedly cutting down and taking several cameras in Lisle.</p><h3></h3><h3><b>What’s being done to address concerns?</b></h3><p>Legislation aimed at bolstering protections has been proposed to the Illinois General Assembly.</p><p>One bill, known as the <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=HB&DocNum=5151&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=166766" target="_blank" ><u>Automated License Plate Recognition System Act</u></a>, would require annual audits and set stricter statewide standards for acceptable use. Another would establish criminal charges for misuse and transparency requirements clarifying which municipalities have plate readers. Neither bill has advanced out of committee.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/abortion/2025/06/12/license-plate-readers-illinois-abortion-immigration" >Mount Prospect police probed for sharing Illinois license plate reader data in Texas abortion case</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" >Former Holiday Hills police chief charged with making nearly 300 unauthorized searches: court records</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2025/08/26/license-plate-camera-company-halts-cooperation-with-federal-agencies-among-investigation-concerns" >License plate camera company halts cooperation with federal agencies amid legal concerns</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Flock license plate readers turn Chicago suburbs into ground zero for bitter fight over surveillance
entries.summary: <p>William Copp was given broad access to Flock Safety’s powerful license-plate reader system as a part-time police officer in Prairie Grove, a small village about an hour northwest of Chicago.</p><p>Flock’s cameras track every driver that passes them, logging billions of license-plate scans in databases that can potentially be searched by any law enforcement agency that pays for access.</p><p>Prosecutors in McHenry County now say Copp was using Flock to stalk his former partners and others in his orbit, conducting hundreds of searches tracking their movements.</p><p>“He knows everything about me,” one of them said in a petition for a protective order. “It scares me to death that he could still be using another system to track me.”</p><p>Law enforcement officials say Flock’s system helps crack cases by allowing them to easily pinpoint crime suspects. But critics argue the technology has largely gone unchecked and is ripe for abuse.</p><p>Copp, who also served as chief of the Holiday Hills Police Department, is among the dozens of police officials class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Freddy Martinez helps run Lucy Parsons Labs, a digital privacy rights group based in Chicago.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Lucy Parsons Labs</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The audit also found that data from Forest Park’s Motorola Solutions plate readers was shared with U.S. Customs and Border Protection.</p><p>Chicago-based Motorola Solutions, which has also provided plate readers to the Chicago Police Department and Illinois State Police, has since said it cut off the agency’s access to cameras in Illinois and taken steps to ensure state laws aren’t broken. Flock announced similar measures.</p><p>Freddy Martinez, co-executive director of Lucy Parsons Lab, said he remains skeptical.</p><p>“All these data privacy laws and the Illinois TRUST Act are effectively unenforceable,” Martinez said. “It’s impossible to know where your data ends up and who is accessing it for legitimate reasons or otherwise.</p><p>“There is no meaningful way to prevent these kinds of abuses when the entire business model depends on massive amounts of data collection.”</p><h3><b>Legislation stalls in Springfield</b></h3><p>Scrutiny of license plate readers has grown as Flock has built up its massive network, but law enforcement agencies in Illinois have long used the technology.</p><p>Chicago cops have had plate readers since at least 2006, although a department spokesperson said it doesn’t have an active contract with Flock.</p><p>The Tamara Clayton Expressway Camera Act, named for the victim of a deadly shooting on Interstate 57, was passed in 2020, giving the state police money for its own plate readers.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker has since poured millions more dollars into the program, adding counties while allowing searches to be used to investigate more crimes.</p><p>The state police has 588 Motorola plate readers statewide, about 300 of which are on Cook County’s expressways and DuSable Lake Shore Drive, according to the state police. While the cameras have scanned more than three billion vehicles over the past year, the hit rate for flagged vehicles was less than 3%.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-8e0000" name="image-8e0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c66a944/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2F80%2Fb3be5a224513949907a0d3e4b040%2Fflockexplainer-2608040071.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/268c5e2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2F80%2Fb3be5a224513949907a0d3e4b040%2Fflockexplainer-2608040071.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ccb8aa5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2F80%2Fb3be5a224513949907a0d3e4b040%2Fflockexplainer-2608040071.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="A Flock Safety camera aimed at traffic in downtown Highland Park, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ccb8aa5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2F80%2Fb3be5a224513949907a0d3e4b040%2Fflockexplainer-2608040071.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/47c6edf/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2F80%2Fb3be5a224513949907a0d3e4b040%2Fflockexplainer-2608040071.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ccb8aa5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2d%2F80%2Fb3be5a224513949907a0d3e4b040%2Fflockexplainer-2608040071.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A Flock Safety camera aimed at traffic in downtown Highland Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Passing legislation that ensures more oversight has proved challenging.</p><p>Bennett, of the ACLU of Illinois, said a key sticking point has been the amount of time that data can be held. Advocates have called for a three-day retention period, but police have pushed for more — with some asking to keep it in perpetuity.</p><p>Members of the General Assembly have now proposed the Automated License Plate Recognition System Act, which would require annual audits and set stricter statewide standards for acceptable plate reader use.</p><p>Another pending bill would regulate what the technology can be used for, establish criminal charges for misuse and clarify which municipalities have plate readers and how the data is used.</p><p>Both pieces of legislation would set shorter data storage limits than the 90 days the state police allows or the year dictated by Chicago police policy. The bills haven’t advanced out of committee.</p><p>“When law enforcement leans more on surveillance tools than being in their communities, it’s really important to assess if it’s really working as it’s intended," Bennett said.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/20/former-holiday-hills-police-chief-charged-with-making-nearly-300-unauthorized-searches-court-records" target="_blank" >Former Holiday Hills police chief charged with making nearly 300 unauthorized searches: court records</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/28/flock-license-plate-reader-lisle-bob-berlin" target="_blank" >3 charged with stealing, vandalizing Flock license plate readers in west suburbs</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/4/20/22911110/chicago-surveillance-camera-automated-license-plates-reader-alpr" target="_blank" >CPD’s growing use of cameras that read license plates leads to worries about data misuse</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Bears pre-practice updates: RT Darnell Wright good to go; DE Austin Booker, DT Gervon Dexter out
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> are practicing with the Titans on Thursday morning at Vanderbilt Health Football Center, their second joint practice of training camp. The teams will play their final preseason game against each other Saturday at Nissan Stadium.</p><p>Bears coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> spoke with reporters before practice and had some updates:</p><p>• Right tackle Darnell Wright hurt his right elbow in practice Tuesday, but the Bears were fortunate to avoid any significant injury. "It was an [aggravation] of some things that went on last year," Johnson said. "He'll be an active participant today." Wright played through a torn UCL in that elbow most of last season.</p><p>• Defensive tackle Gervon Dexter, who has been at the center of trade speculation this week, did not travel with the team to Nashville. Johnson said he has a hamstring injury.</p><p>• Defensive end Austin Booker is "banged up" with a groin injury and Johnson said he's week-to-week.</p><p>• Recently added defensive end Marcus Davenport has yet to practice, but isn't injured. Johnson said the team is "being smart with him [because] he's a player that's missed a lot of time over the last three years." He's been working on the side with the strength and conditioning staff.</p><p>• Rookie cornerback Malik Muhammad currently is in line to start at nickel unless Kyler Gordon returns for the opener, and Johnson feels good about that position even as Muhammad goes through "bumps in the road." He said the Bears are "really pleased with the path that he's on right now."</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Bears-Titans notes: Chicago native Carnell Tate torches former favorite team
entries.summary: <p>NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Titans receiver <b>Carnell Tate </b>grew up loving the Bears.</p><p>“<b>Jay Cutler </b>— we love Jay Cutler out there,” the Titans receiver said Thursday. “<b>Matt Forte</b>, B-Marsh.”</p><p>His love for Cutler, Forte and wide receiver <b>Brandon Marshall </b>came from his father.</p><p>“My dad was Chicago Bears fan,” he said. “Still is, except when we play them.”</p><p>Tate grew up in Garfield Park.He enrolled at Marist, where he was promoted from the freshman team to the varsity after just four games. In 2021, he transferred to IMG Academy. A year later, he committed to Ohio State. In April, the Titans took him No. 4 overall — the highest pick they’ve ever used for a wideout.</p><p>On Thursday, he dominated a depleted Bears defensive backfield. He caught seven passes, two for touchdowns, in the joint practice.</p><p>“He was open, honestly, giving me a step on the defender,” quarterback <b>Cam Ward </b>said. “Then me and him also continue to grow together, with me putting the ball in the radius where he can make a play on it. And him also making a play on it when I’m not as accurate. . . .</p><p>“He showed why he was that pick.”</p><p><b>D-line depth down</b></p><p>Bears defensive end <b>Austin Booker </b>is working through a groin injury and is “week-to-week,” coach <b>Ben Johnson</b> said, putting his status for Week 1 in question.</p><p>The Bears signed <b>Marcus Davenport </b>to give them added defensive line depth, but he still isn’t practicing, either. Davenport, who was added Aug. 17, isn’t dealing with any specific injury, Johnson said, but is ramping up.</p><p>“He’s a player that’s missed a lot of time over the last three years,” Johnson said, “and so he’s being integrated into the program.”</p><p><b>Will they play?</b></p><p>Both Johnson and quarterback <b>Caleb Williams </b>were non-committal about whether the quarterback — or other starters — would play in Saturday’s exhibition finale.</p><p>“I don’t know if I’m playing,” Williams said, “so whatever coach says.”</p><p>The Bears, he said, would weigh the quality and quantity of the joint practice reps in making a decision. Starters played a lot — in high temperatures — Thursday.</p><p>The Titans will play their starters, though coach <b>Robert Saleh </b>said joint practices were far more like regular-season games than any of the preseason games were.</p><p><b>Notes</b></p><p>The flashiest moment of practice was when Williams handed the ball to <b>D’Andre Swift</b>, who threw a lateral back to Williams on the left flank.</p><p>“That was a pretty good toss, too,” Williams said.</p><p>Williams when launched a pass up the left sideline to receiver <b>Rome Odunze.</b></p><p>• Right tackle <b>Darnell Wright </b>practiced in full two days after he aggravated the right elbow injury that forced him to wear a brace for most of the season.</p><p>• Former Bills coach <b>Sean McDermott </b>visited practice, as did former Titans cornerback <b>Pacman Jones</b>.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true"
