entries.title: Pete's Market to be built as part of redevelopment of former site of Stateway Gardens
entries.summary: <p>McLaurin Development Partners cleared the first hurdle to redevelop the former Stateway Gardens site into a housing and retail destination, anchored by a much-needed grocery store.</p><p>The Chicago Plan Commission gave initial city approvals to the developer's $70 million plan Aug. 20. If approved by the City Council, construction on the Bronzeville project will start early next year, wrapping up by mid-2028. The project would create 150 temporary construction jobs and 225 permanent jobs.</p><p>McLaurin, whose projects include the forthcoming Englewood Connect and the redevelopment of the former Michael Reese Hospital site, wants to complete the project in two phases. </p><p>The first phase would include the retail portion, anchored by a 70,000-square-foot Pete's Market. Plans for the site, south of Pershing Road and abutting the Dan Ryan Expressway, call for a medical office for outpatient care, a hardware store, a restaurant, a bank and other uses. It will have 378 parking spaces, many of them in front of the grocer. McLaurin will also add landscaping at Pershing and State streets to soften the appearance of the retail center, along with trees between the project site and the Dan Ryan.</p><p>The second phase, north of Pershing Road, would include up to 551 apartments, according to plans submitted to the City Council. McLaurin will price 20% of the units in Phase 2 as affordable, under the city's Affordable Requirements Ordinance.</p><p>Third Ward Ald. Pat Dowell said on Facebook that there’s a letter of intent for the Chicago-based Pete’s Market to occupy the project.</p><p>McLaurin didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>Pete’s started on the South Side during the 1970s as a small full-service produce stand. Its fruit and vegetables continue to be handpicked and delivered daily, according to Pete’s website. Each store has a full-service kitchen, bakery and deli.</p><p>Pete’s has locations across Chicago and its suburbs, with many on the South and West sides. </p><p>Its Bronzeville location will be a welcome addition to the neighborhood, if approved. And it would come at a time when grocers across the South and West sides like <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" >Save A Lot</a> have shuttered in recent years, leaving predominantly Black and Brown neighborhoods without a nearby grocery store.</p><p>Stateway Gardens was a public housing development along the Dan Ryan, north of the Robert Taylor Homes. It was built by the Chicago Housing Authority between 1955 and 1958.</p><p>Demolition of the mid- and high-rise buildings in the Stateway and Robert Taylor projects started in 1998 and was completed by 2007, as part of the CHA's Plan for Transformation that pledged to tear down and rebuild tens of thousands of CHA-subsidized units at developments with affordable and market-rate apartments.</p>

entries.title: How to enjoy tonight's lunar eclipse from Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Thursday night, Chicagoans will have the opportunity to witness a lunar eclipse — a rare alignment between the sun, the moon and the stars.</p><p>More than 96% of the moon will be obscured by earth’s shadow and could turn a deep red color, the reason for the nickname “blood moon.”</p><p>“Every lunar eclipse is special,” said Hunter Miller, public observing educator at the Adler Planetarium. “We don’t get them super often… Anytime the lunar eclipse happens, especially one with this much coverage, it’s going to be exciting.”</p><p>For those looking to catch a glimpse of the eclipse, this is your chance — the next full eclipse of the moon isn’t until 2029. Follow these tips from astronomy experts to get the best view.</p><p><b>When is the eclipse happening?</b></p><p>The partial eclipse will start around 9:30 p.m. Thursday with the maximum coverage around 11:15 p.m., Miller said.</p><p>This is earlier than many eclipses that happen around 2 or 3 a.m., Miller said.</p><p>“This is one of those times where you said we really will have the best seat because we won’t have to get up at oh-dark-thirty hours,” Michelle Nichols, Adler Planetarium’s director of public observing, told Sasha Ann Simons on WBEZ’s ‘In the Loop.’</p><p>The eclipse will end at 12:58 a.m. Friday, Nichols said.</p><p><b>What exactly is a lunar eclipse?</b></p><p>A lunar eclipse occurs when the Earth’s shadow obscures all or part of the moon.</p><p>Thursday’s eclipse is a partial eclipse, meaning the entire moon won’t be in Earth’s shadow, but at 96%, the eclipse can be described as near-total.</p><p>A total lunar eclipse stretched over the Americas, Australia and eastern Asia in March.</p><p>A lunar eclipse is not to be confused with a solar eclipse, which occurs when the moon aligns directly between the sun and the Earth, blocking sunlight from reaching the Earth. A total solar eclipse occurred earlier this year, but most of the Americas missed out on the view as its path was centered over Europe.</p><p><b>How do I make sure I have a good view?</b></p><p>The moon won’t be that high in the sky, so people hoping to see it need to make sure they have a good view to the south and southeast.</p><p>This eclipse doesn’t require a dark sky, so it’s a good opportunity for people who live in cities like Chicago and deal with light pollution to see an eclipse.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> </div><p>Chicago isn’t alone in keeping its eyes on the sky. Billions across North and South America, Europe, Africa and the Middle East will be able to see the eclipsed moon, provided the skies are clear, the Associated Press reported.</p><p><b>Do I need any special tools or equipment?</b></p><p>Unlike a solar eclipse, which can damage your eyes if you look directly at it without special glasses, a lunar eclipse can be enjoyed with the naked eye.</p><p>A telescope or binoculars could provide a better view with more detail of the moon, but they’re certainly not necessary.</p><p><b>Why does the moon turn red?</b></p><p>The red color cast on the moon is more than just a shadow, Miller says.</p><p>“That color is the reflected light of every single sunrise and sunset happening on the Earth in that moment,” Miller said. “So that light that curves around the edges of the Earth strikes its surface, creating that stunning red color, and it’s such a beautiful connection between our home here on Earth and the moon in the night sky.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Marie Mendoza and Sasha-Ann Simons.</i></p>

entries.title: Motorist accused in fatal motorcycle hit-and-run in Ashburn left cell phone on scene
entries.summary: <p>A man was released pending trial Thursday after being accused of driving recklessly and leaving the scene of an accident that left a motorcyclist dead in July, officials said.</p><p>Darryl Short, 45, appeared before a Cook County judge who released him pending trial, court records show. Short is charged with reckless homicide and leaving the scene of an accident that killed Churone Walls, 47.</p><p>The wreck happened July 24 in the 2200 block of West 79th Street, according to police.</p><p>Walls was driving a three-wheeled motorcycle west on 79th Street at about 7 p.m. when Short, also westbound, blew a stop sign while driving 63 mph and attempted to pass Walls, crashing into her, prosecutors said in court. </p><p>Short's Volkswagen Atlas went airborne before landing on Walls and her motorcycle. The SUV then dragged Walls and her motorcycle until Short plowed into a light pole and came to a stop, prosecutors said. </p><p>Short then left the scene in another vehicle, but left his cell phone in the Atlas, prosecutors said. The phone, registered to Short, showed he made no 911 calls on the night of the crash.</p><p>Short has traffic violations as well as convictions for unlawful use of a weapon and a drug-related offense. He is due back in court on Sept. 16.</p>

entries.title: Sky forward Rickea Jackson is choosing to bedazzle her ACL rehab
entries.summary: <p>When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> forward Rickea Jackson tore her ACL earlier this season, her former Unrivaled teammate Paige Bueckers offered some advice.</p><p>If Jackson wanted to make it through rehab, Bueckers told her, she needed to give her knee a name.</p><p>“Even if it’s just a knee, you have to make that knee feel loved,” Bueckers said while discussing injury recovery on the 'Bird’s Eye View' podcast. “I’m a huge believer in the power of the tongue. How you speak to yourself really manifests.”</p><p>Jackson took the advice and, with her usual charm, came up with the perfect name: “Ricknee-a.”</p><p>The break from basketball also has forced her to pick up new hobbies. Her favorite: bedazzling. She finds it therapeutic, but it also helps when her motivation starts to wane.</p><p>Take the ice machine she uses on her Ricknee-a. It’s red and ugly, and Jackson hates icing in the first place. So she and Sky basketball operations manager Maggie Maloney came up with an idea: Maybe Jackson would use it more if they bedazzled it.</p><p>Now that the machine looks cute, Jackson does.</p><p>It’s all part of the process. Jackson is committed to putting in the work, day after day. That doesn’t mean she finds it particularly thrilling.</p><p>“My trainer and my strength coach, they’re always telling me where I PR at,” Jackson said. “They’re more excited about the little gains than I am. I just be like, ‘OK, I can bend my knee. Woohoo.’”</p><p>One can understand the lack of enthusiasm for a knee bend given what Jackson had been doing on the court before the injury. She averaged 22 points in the three games before tearing her ACL, maybe on track for her first All-Star appearance.</p><p>According to assistant coach Latricia Trammell, who’d coached her with the Sparks, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/15/rickea-jackson-looks-empowered-in-the-sky-offense" >Jackson looked at peace</a> in Chicago. A much-deserved turn after an incident involving her ex-boyfriend, Falcons defensive end James Pearce Jr., who was charged with battery and stalking after allegedly ramming his car repeatedly into hers as she drove toward a police station.</p><p>Jackson was in a better place, personally and professionally. Then basketball was taken away.</p><p>It hasn’t been easy, but she’s trying to see the good in the interruption. Like the chance to wear her nails longer and get more mileage out of her hairstyles. Oh, and some space to discover who she is off the court.</p><p>“Since seventh grade, everything has literally been basketball,” Jackson said. “When I go out of the country, it’s basketball.</p><p>“God felt like I needed to take a break from basketball. He felt like I needed to really feel everything that I was going through off the court and handle things like that.”</p><p>For once, Jackson has had an opportunity to be “a regular person.” The time away also has allowed her to see basketball from a -different vantage point.</p><p>From the sideline, she’s studying teammates, picking up defensive skills she wants to incorporate: DiJonai Carrington’s active hands and the way Natasha Cloud navigates screens.</p><p>She also has relished the breakout of -undrafted rookie guard Sydney Taylor.</p><p>“I called it,” Jackson said, cheesing at the mention of Taylor. “I told y’all in training camp: ‘I don’t know who this woman is, but she can dunk.’</p><p>“I’m so excited for her. She’s truly getting the fruits of her labor. I feel like people are truly starting to know who Sydney Taylor is, and I’m so happy for her.”</p><p>That the Sky fell short of their playoff goal hasn’t shaken Jackson’s belief in what they’re building. She is confident the team is better than its record suggests and sees herself, Taylor and Kamilla Cardoso as the young foundation of a future championship contender.</p><p>Asked what she envisions for the franchise, Jackson did not lack ambition.</p><p>“I see a hardworking team, a gritty team,” she said. “I see a flow state of wins strung together. I feel like it could be a dynasty.</p><p>“We want to get back to the 2021 championship ways. Rome wasn’t built in a day, so it’s going to take time. But I’m willing to do my part to make sure the Sky turn into a dynasty.”</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Anthony Rizzo takes next step in broadcasting as booth analyst for Reds-Cubs on NBC's 'Sunday Night Baseball'
entries.summary: <p>NBC is learning about Anthony Rizzo what Cubs fans already knew.</p><p>“His personality is infectious,” NBC Sports senior producer Matt Borzello told the Sun-Times. “I can see why he was such a fan favorite in Chicago.”</p><p>Rizzo has taken to his burgeoning second career as a TV analyst quite well, impressing colleagues and executives with his insights and work ethic. He’ll take another step Sunday when he debuts in the broadcast booth to call the Reds-Cubs game on NBC’s “Sunday Night Baseball.”</p><p>The star first baseman for the Cubs’ 2016 World Series champions, Rizzo began his broadcasting career this year as a field analyst for NBC’s “Inside the Pitch” feature. The plan was to put him in the booth twice to help prepare him to call a wild-card series, all four of which will air on NBC.</p><p>A scheduling conflict limited him to one game in the booth, and when NBC flipped Reds-Cubs with Astros-Mets a month ago, flexing the Cubs into prime time, Rizzo’s first game as a booth analyst became a “Sunday Night Baseball” broadcast.</p><p>Rizzo will be the Cubs analyst alongside Reds analyst Jeff Brantley and play-by-play voice Jason Benetti. Former Reds first baseman Joey Votto will be the “Inside the Pitch” analyst.</p><p>How will Rizzo prepare for the new role?</p><p>“Just ask questions,” Rizzo told the Sun-Times. “Lean on Jason Benetti, lean on the NBC crew. I am very in tune with the Cubs. It’s basically speaking my language talking about them. It’s just a little bit more in depth on the stats and how guys have been doing, more making sure all of that’s readily available — so it sounds like I know what I’m talking about.”</p><p>Rizzo was effusive in his praise for Benetti, the former White Sox TV voice, calling him the captain for the ship.</p><p>“Jason Benetti’s a great leader,” Rizzo said. “He basically directs all of it in the best way, making sure it’s a broadcast and not necessarily a podcast. I enjoy it, and I hope there’s times where people learn something or think of something in a different way. Hopefully, that’s what I can bring to the table.”</p><p>Borzello said he has, pointing to a recent broadcast in which Rizzo, as the field analyst, broke down Phillies star and former Cubs slugger Kyle Schwarber’s at-bats. Rizzo explained how Schwarber’s first at-bat set him up for his second, in which he homered.</p><p>“His insight in knowing situational baseball is remarkable,” said Borzello, the lead producer for “Sunday Night Baseball.” “He’s definitely a Cubs expert. He talks to the players and coaches all the time. We had a production call the other day, and he was talking about he spoke with Ian Happ and one of the coaches. We had a couple of questions, he said, ‘Hey, let me follow up.’ ”</p><p>But going from playing baseball to talking baseball isn’t easy. Borzello said Rizzo is being taught to get to his point quickly because what he says first is what the audience will hear.</p><p>“I’ve had a lot of help behind the scenes from Bruce Cornblatt, who’s with NBC, who’s been in the industry a long time, coaching me up, how to deliver what I’m trying to say,” Rizzo said. “The challenge has been the delivery at times. But there’s nothing but positive feedback. It’s just little adjustments that you make.</p><p>“It’s what I took into baseball: Nothing is ever going to be perfect. I’m really striving for perfection, but I just want to be really good all the time.”</p><p>Borzello is looking forward to hearing the banter between Rizzo and Votto, who competed against each other in the National League Central for almost a decade.</p><p>“With Votto and Rizzo, you’ve got two of the best first basemen of their generation and two of the best personalities,” Borzello said. “There’s such a mutual respect between those two.”</p><p>Borzello also is looking forward to working more with Rizzo, who has contributed to Netflix’s baseball coverage, as well.</p><p>“This is not just a one-off for him,” Borzello said. “He wants to be better and better every week. There’s no doubt this will be an excellent second career for him, not just a little side gig.”</p><p>Said Rizzo: “It’s been the perfect amount, honestly. I’m around it as much as I want to be, and I’m away from it as much as I want to be. It’s good to be able to talk the game, to be around the game and do it on my own terms.”</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p>NBC 5 hired <b>Natalie Spala</b> as weekend sports anchor/reporter. She’ll start next week. Spala, a native of Livonia, Mich., arrives from WJLA-TV, the ABC affiliate in Washington. Longtime sports anchor <b>Jeff Blanzy</b> will continue to fill in. Also, beginning in September, NBC 5 will air a local sports show at 6:30 weeknights.</p><p>• <b>Ryan Dempster</b>, who was named to the Cubs’ 150th anniversary team, and <b>Kevin Millar</b> will co-host MLB Network’s “Intentional Talk” at Wrigley Field from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. Friday.</p><p>• <b>Jason Goff</b> soon will launch the podcast “Jason Goff: Unscripted” with 312 Sports, the platform that carries <b>Dan Bernstein’s</b> shows. Goff also will host a twice-weekly national football show.</p><p>• Proving the shortsightedness of Nexstar’s decision to lay him off in February, <b>Chris Boden</b> is back for fill-in work at WGN-TV and Radio as the sports calendar gets busy.</p><p>• The Brewers-Cubs game Thursday will air exclusively on Fox. entries.title: Emmett Till, Dr. King, Obama and Aug. 28
entries.summary: <p>I’ve been trying to connect a lot of dots in my pursuit of former President Barack Obama’s famous tan suit. But here’s the tricky part about connecting dots, even for me, an experienced journalist: First, you’ve got to find them.</p><p>Let me explain.</p><p>I’m <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tansuit" >on the hunt</a> for the tan suit Obama wore to a White House press conference in 2014 — the one that sparked attacks from right-wing critics eager to diminish the nation’s first Black president. The suit is not in the recently opened museum at the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park; reporters were told Obama gave it away years ago after cleaning out his closet.</p><p>If you saw the former president wearing a tan suit when he played himself opposite Larry David in the August finale of HBO’s “Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness” in a spoof about that press conference — well, it’s a look-alike, not the original.</p><p>The entire saga sparked questions about race, culture, what’s news and, yes, presidential fashion. Questions as relevant in 2026 as they were in 2014. Questions I am asking as part of my search for the tan suit — and the conversations I hope to be having with you.</p><p>Recently, I was talking about my pursuit with Tavis Smiley, the host of a nationally syndicated talk show aimed at Black audiences. And I’m grateful to Smiley for offering up a generous serving of dots when I was a guest on his Aug. 19 <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TvUVekecGHo" target="_blank" ><u>show</u></a>.</p><p>During the segment, I mentioned the anniversary of the tan suit press conference is Aug. 28.</p><p>“You know what else happened on Aug. 28?” he asked. “Think about it.”</p><p>I was stumped.</p><p>“Being a history buff, my mind went to that same date,” Smiley said. “Here’s what else happened on Aug. 28.”</p><p>On Aug. 28, 1955, Emmett Till, a 14-year-old Black youth from Chicago’s South Side, was kidnapped and savagely murdered by two white supremacists in Mississippi. Till’s mutilated body was pulled from the Tallahatchie River on Aug. 31, 1955, with barbed wire tied around his neck and attached to a cotton gin fan weighing 70 pounds.</p><p>Till’s killing was a defining moment in civil rights history due to a key decision by his mother, Mamie Till-Mobley. She insisted on an open casket for her son’s funeral at the Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, 4021 S. State St., so the world could see his mutilated body and witness the results of race-based violence.</p><p>On Aug. 28, 1963, Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. delivered his “I Have a Dream” speech. Standing on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, King called for racial justice.</p><p>“Now is the time to rise from the dark and desolate valley of segregation to the sunlit path of racial justice. Now is the time to lift our nation from the quicksand of racial injustice to the solid rock of brotherhood. Now is the time to make justice a reality to all of God’s children. … I have a dream that one day, even the state of Mississippi, a state sweltering with the heat of oppression, will be transformed into an oasis of freedom and justice.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d20000" name="module-d20000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Pursuit of the Suit</h3><br>On Aug. 28, 2014, the tan suit that then-President Barack Obama wore to a White House press conference became an unexpected story. After his presidency, Obama reportedly gave the suit away cleaning out his closet. Follow as former Sun-Times Washington Bureau Chief <b>Lynn Sweet</b> hunts down the original tan suit — and what makes it so compelling along the way.<br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-dddea0e2-a259-11f1-9f97-593067e43792"><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/17/hunt-for-barack-obamas-tan-suit-help-us-find-it" target="_blank" ><b>We’re on the hunt for Barack Obama’s tan suit. Help us find it.</b></a></li><li><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2026/08/27/emmett-till-dr-martin-luther-king-jr-mlk-barack-obama-tavis-smiley-pursuit-tan-suit" ><b>Emmett Till, Dr. King, Obama and Aug. 28</b></a></li><li>Coming soon: The Original Suit</li><li>Coming soon: The Replica</li></ul></div> </div><p>On Aug. 28, 2008, Sen. Barack Obama, D-Ill., accepted the Democratic nomination for president. Obama delivered his acceptance speech at Denver’s Invesco Field, home of the NFL’s Broncos. His words take on special meaning today: This summer, the nation marks its 250th anniversary as President Donald Trump dismantles racial equity gains and ends racial justice programs and policies.</p><p>Obama noted in Denver that he was speaking at the nation’s 232nd anniversary and “at each moment when that promise was in jeopardy, ordinary men and women, students and soldiers, farmers and teachers, nurses and janitors, found the courage to keep it alive.”</p><p>“We meet at one of those defining moments,” he continued. “A moment when our nation is at war, our economy is in turmoil and the American promise has been threatened once more. That’s the promise of America — the idea that we are responsible for ourselves, but that we also rise or fall as one nation; the fundamental belief that I am my brother’s keeper; I am my sister’s keeper.”</p><p>And on Aug. 28, 2014, Obama wore that tan suit to a press conference to discuss the economy, war and global crises, with the takeaway being his choice of clothing. That press conference prompted questions about whether race was a factor in the overheated outrage over the summer suit worn by the first Black president.</p><p>See how these Aug. 28 threads weave together?</p><p>The Obama Presidential Foundation is leaning into the tan suit. Last week, it posted on social media, “We heard Tan Suit Day is coming up… Show us your tan suit.” It’s a callout for folks to share their “favorite tan suit look” on social media.</p><p>I didn’t know Tan Suit Day was a thing.</p><p>Now I do.</p><p>I’ve got another dot.</p>
